meta.name: Main Street Agent
meta.tagline: Plain-language help with banking, starting and growing a business, marketing, and staying safe with money.
meta.disclaimer: Main Street Agent explains how common money and business processes usually work and points you to the right institution or professional. It is not financial, legal or tax advice, and it does not tell anyone how to invest. Fees, rates and rules change, so confirm every number with the institution or agency before you act.

entries.title: Opening a business bank account
entries.summary: Keep business money separate. Most banks ask for an EIN or SSN, formation documents and ID; fintech options like Novo charge no monthly fee.
body: A separate business account makes taxes, bookkeeping and getting paid much easier, even for a sole proprietor or freelancer. Banks must verify the business and the people who own or control it.

Expect to provide: an EIN (free from the IRS) or your SSN if you are a sole proprietor, formation documents for an LLC or corporation (such as articles of organization), any business license or DBA filing, and photo ID for each owner.

Options include big banks with branches and cash deposits, local credit unions, and online fintech platforms. Novo, for example, is a fintech, not a bank; its banking services are provided by Middlesex Federal Savings, F.A., Member FDIC. It advertises no-fee business checking with invoicing, free standard ACH transfers, QuickBooks integration and ATM fee reimbursement up to $7 a month per account.
Fintech business accounts are often weaker on cash deposits and in-person help. If you handle a lot of cash, compare a bank with branches.
steps: Get an EIN from IRS.gov (free) if you have an LLC, corporation or employees.
Gather formation documents, any DBA and ID for each owner.
Compare one big bank, one credit union and one fintech on fees, cash deposits and integrations.
Open the account and route all business income and expenses through it.

details.Documents: EIN or SSN, formation docs, ID for owners

entries.next_step: Get your free EIN, then compare a fintech and a branch bank based on how much cash you handle.

entries.title: Before you start: why, when, where and how
entries.summary: Four honest questions to answer before you spend real money: why this business, when you can afford to be wrong, where you already have an edge, and how to sell before you build.
body: A business makes sense when it solves a specific problem for specific people. Wanting freedom or a bigger income is a good motivation, but it isn't a business by itself. Start from a problem you understand well, ideally one you have lived or seen up close.
The right time is when you can survive being wrong for a while. That usually means some savings, or keeping your job and testing the idea on nights and weekends until it proves itself.
Where means both market and format: online or in person, product or service. Pick a place where you already have some credibility, access or skill, even a small one.

How comes down to selling before building. Get the simplest version in front of one paying customer before you invest in the polished version. The concrete starter kit is four things: a legal entity (or a sole proprietorship to start), a separate bank account, a way to take payment, and asking a real person for money in exchange for something.
steps: Write the problem you solve in one sentence, using your customer's words.
Decide how many months you can test this without risking rent or bills.
List three advantages you already have: skills, contacts, location or experience.
Offer the simplest version to ten real people and ask for payment.

details.When: When you can afford to be wrong
details.Where: Where you already have an edge

entries.next_step: Write your one-sentence problem statement, then ask ten people who have that problem whether they'd pay for a fix.

entries.title: Making your first dollar from a skill
entries.summary: You don't need a website or a logo to get paid. You need a problem someone cares about, a simple offer that names the result, and the nerve to ask.
body: Most first sales come from three things: a real problem that costs someone time, money or customers; an offer that describes the result rather than your skill; and a direct, polite ask.
Describe the outcome, not the tool. "I'm a video editor" is a skill. "I turn your long videos into short clips you can post every week" is an offer someone can say yes to.
Start conversations, not pitches. A short note that shows you understand their specific problem, and offers to send an idea, gets more replies than a list of your credentials.
Your first dollar is evidence, not the finish line. Use what you learn from the first customer to sharpen the offer, the price or who you target, then do it again.
steps: Pick one problem you can fix this week for a specific type of person.
Write the offer as: "I help [who] get [result] without [pain]."
Send five short, personal messages that name their problem and offer one idea.
Deliver well, ask for a testimonial, and raise the price a little for the next one.

details.You need: A problem, an offer, an ask
details.You don't need: A website, logo or big following

entries.next_step: Write your offer in one sentence and send it to five people who clearly have the problem.

entries.title: Sole proprietorship, LLC or corporation?
entries.summary: A sole proprietorship is the default and costs nothing. An LLC adds a liability shield and costs a state fee. Corporations suit investors and bigger plans.
body: If you sell something on your own without forming anything, you are already a sole proprietor. It costs nothing to start, but there is no legal separation between you and the business, so business debts and lawsuits can reach your personal assets.

A limited liability company (LLC) is formed by filing with your state. It separates the business's liabilities from yours, as long as you actually run it as a separate thing. By default, a single-member LLC's profit is reported on the owner's personal tax return.

Corporations (C corporations, and S corporation tax status) add more formality: shares, a board, meeting records. They tend to suit businesses raising outside investment or with several owners. S corporation status is a tax election that some profitable small businesses use, and it is worth discussing with a CPA before choosing.
None of these changes the need for good habits: separate bank account, written records and the right insurance.

details.S corp: A tax election — ask a CPA

entries.next_step: If you have real customers or real risk, compare your state's LLC filing fee with the cost of a basic liability insurance policy.

entries.title: How to form an LLC, step by step
entries.summary: Pick a state, file articles of organization, get a free EIN, write an operating agreement, name a registered agent, open a business bank account, and keep it in good standing.
body: Most owners form the LLC in their home state, or in the state where the business or asset mainly operates. You can file it yourself with the state, use a formation service, or hire an attorney. All three create the same legal entity; they differ in cost, speed and how much you handle yourself.
Filing articles of organization creates the LLC. Next, get an Employer Identification Number (EIN) directly from the IRS, which is free. Any site that charges for an EIN is not the IRS.

An operating agreement spells out who owns the LLC and how it is run. Not every state requires one on file, but banks, lenders and title companies often ask for it, and it backs up your authority to sign for the business.
Every state requires a registered agent (Arizona calls it a statutory agent) to receive legal papers for the LLC. Then open a business bank account and run every business payment through it.

Forming is the start, not the end. Many states require an annual or biennial report and fee; missing it can get the LLC administratively dissolved, which quietly removes the protection you formed it for.
steps: Check your state's filing fee and name rules on its official business filing site.
File articles of organization, then apply for a free EIN at IRS.gov.
Write and sign an operating agreement, even for a one-person LLC.
Name a registered agent and open a separate business bank account.
Put the state's report deadline, if any, on your calendar.
entries.next_step: Look up your state's LLC filing page, then get your EIN only from IRS.gov.

entries.title: Arizona specifics: LLCs, statutory agents and trade names
entries.summary: Arizona LLCs file with the Arizona Corporation Commission, need a statutory agent, don't file annual reports, and register trade names (DBAs) with the Secretary of State for $10.
body: In Arizona, LLCs file articles of organization with the Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC). Every LLC must name a statutory agent, Arizona's term for a registered agent, and keep that information current; letting it lapse can lead to administrative dissolution.

Arizona does not require LLCs to file an annual report or pay an annual fee, which is unusual. Some new LLCs must publish a notice of formation in a newspaper, but LLCs whose statutory agent is in Maricopa or Pima County are exempt, and the ACC publishes the notice for them.

A trade name (often called a DBA, "doing business as") is registered with the Arizona Secretary of State. The application fee is $10. A trade name lets a business operate under a brand name; it is not a separate legal entity and does not give liability protection by itself.
Banks often ask for a DBA certificate if your business uses a name different from its legal name. Keep a copy with your formation documents.
steps: Search the ACC's business records to make sure your name is available.
File articles of organization with the ACC and name your statutory agent.
If you'll use a brand name, file a trade name application with the Secretary of State.
Keep your statutory agent details current whenever anything changes.

details.Publication: Exempt if agent is in Maricopa or Pima

entries.next_step: Check your exact filing fee and form on azcc.gov before you file; fees change.

entries.title: Registered agents and formation services
entries.summary: Every LLC needs someone to receive legal papers at a physical address. You can be your own agent, or pay a service that also keeps your home address off public records.
body: A registered agent (statutory agent in Arizona) is the person or company named on state records to receive lawsuits and official notices for your LLC during business hours, at a physical address in that state.
You can usually serve as your own agent, but your address becomes public and you must be available. Many owners pay a registered agent service for privacy and reliability.

Formation services such as Northwest Registered Agent, Bizee, ZenBusiness and others bundle filing, the agent role, a business address and compliance reminders. Their prices change and often include first-year discounts, so compare the total cost over two or three years, not just the first-month price.
Watch for mailers that look like official state notices but are really offers to file your annual report for a large fee. The real state agency's address and website are the only ones to trust.

details.Job: Receives legal papers for the LLC
details.DIY: Free, but your address goes public

entries.next_step: Decide whether you want your home address on public records; if not, compare two or three agent services by total yearly cost.

entries.title: EINs, and the end of federal ownership reports for U.S. companies
entries.summary: An EIN is free from the IRS. Since August 2026, U.S.-formed companies no longer file beneficial ownership reports with FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act.
body: An Employer Identification Number is the business's federal tax ID. It is free, and you apply directly on IRS.gov. Banks, payment processors and lenders ask for it.

For a while, most small LLCs and corporations had to report their owners to FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act. FinCEN first suspended that for domestic companies in March 2025, then issued a final rule that took effect on August 14, 2026, permanently exempting companies formed in the United States and their U.S. owners.

Foreign companies registered to do business in a U.S. state still have a narrower reporting duty. And separate rules still apply elsewhere, such as FinCEN's reporting of certain all-cash residential real estate purchases by entities.
If a letter or email says you owe a fee to file a "BOI report" for your U.S. LLC, treat it as a likely scam.
entries.next_step: Get your EIN only at IRS.gov, and ignore paid "BOI filing" notices for a U.S. LLC.

entries.title: Keep business money separate (or lose the shield)
entries.summary: An LLC protects you only if you treat it as separate. Mixing personal and business money is the most common reason courts ignore the LLC.
body: Courts can "pierce the veil" and hold an owner personally liable when the owner treats the LLC as a personal piggy bank: paying personal bills from the business account, depositing business income personally, or skipping basic records.
Personal guarantees follow you no matter whose name is on the title. If a lender required your signature, that debt is yours too.
The LLC also doesn't cover your own actions. If you personally cause harm, for example while driving, you can be named alongside the LLC.
The fix is boring and effective: one business bank account, one business card, every business payment through them, and a simple monthly record of what came in and went out.

details.Habit: One account, one card, monthly records

entries.next_step: Move every business payment and deposit into one dedicated business account starting this month.

entries.title: Chase Business Complete Banking
entries.summary: Chase's main small-business checking: a $15 monthly fee that can be waived, built-in card acceptance (QuickAccept) and same-day deposits from card sales.
body: Chase Business Complete Banking is the entry small-business checking account at Chase. Its monthly service fee is $15, and Chase lists ways to bring it to $0, including keeping a $2,000 minimum daily balance or receiving at least $2,000 a month in deposits from Chase QuickAccept and other Chase payment products.
QuickAccept lets you take card payments with your phone, and card sales can land in the account as soon as the same day at no extra cost.

To open, Chase asks for information on each owner with 10% or more of the business, a tax ID (EIN, or SSN for sole proprietors), formation documents such as articles of organization, and a DBA certificate if the business uses a different name. Older LLCs may also be asked for a certificate of good standing from the state.
Chase also offers larger tiers (Performance and Platinum Business Checking) with higher fees and higher waiver balances, built for businesses with more transactions and cash deposits.

details.Waiver examples: $2,000 min daily balance, or $2,000+ in Chase payment deposits
details.Bring: EIN, formation docs, ID, DBA if any

entries.next_step: Gather your articles of organization, EIN letter and ID, and confirm the current waiver options on chase.com before applying.

entries.title: Taxes when you work for yourself
entries.summary: Self-employed people pay income tax plus 15.3% self-employment tax, usually through quarterly estimated payments. Payment-app income is taxable whether or not you get a form.
body: When you work for yourself, nobody withholds taxes from your pay. Besides income tax, you owe self-employment tax of 15.3% on net earnings (12.4% Social Security, up to a yearly wage cap, plus 2.9% Medicare).
Most people pay this through quarterly estimated payments, generally due in mid-April, mid-June, mid-September and mid-January. Missing them can bring penalties.

Payment apps and marketplaces send a Form 1099-K only above a reporting threshold, which went back to more than $20,000 and more than 200 transactions per year under 2025 tax law. All business income is taxable even if you never receive a form.

Keep receipts and a simple monthly ledger. Ordinary business expenses reduce taxable profit, but only with records to back them up. If you are unsure, free IRS-certified help is available through VITA for many filers.
steps: Open a separate savings account and move 25–30% of each payment into it for taxes.
Track income and expenses monthly in a spreadsheet or bookkeeping app.
Calendar the four estimated-payment dates and pay through IRS Direct Pay.
Ask a tax professional or VITA volunteer to check your first year.
entries.next_step: Start a tax savings account today and set aside part of every business payment.

entries.title: Building business credit
entries.summary: A new LLC has no credit history. Lenders usually want one to three years of activity before lending without your personal guarantee.
body: A brand-new LLC looks very different to a lender than a two-year-old one. The entity doesn't create credit; the history you build inside it does.

Common steps: register with a business credit bureau, open net-30 vendor accounts and a business credit card that report to commercial bureaus, pay everything on time from the business account, and let revenue flow through that account consistently.
Until there's history, most lenders ask for a personal guarantee, which means the debt follows you even though the LLC is the borrower.
Be wary of companies selling "instant business credit" or "shelf" companies with fake history. Lenders look at real revenue, tax returns and payment records.
entries.next_step: Open one business credit card or vendor account that reports to commercial bureaus, and pay it in full every month.

entries.title: Putting a vehicle in your LLC's name
entries.summary: You can retitle a car you own to your LLC or buy one through it. You'll need commercial insurance, and only genuine business use is deductible.
body: Moving a car you already own into the LLC is a title transfer at the DMV, usually with a bill of sale, the current title, the LLC's articles and proof of insurance. If the car still has a loan, the lender must agree, and some require you to refinance in the LLC's name.

Buying through the LLC means the business is the buyer from day one: pay from the business account, use the dealer's commercial or fleet desk, and expect a new LLC to need your personal guarantee for financing.
A vehicle titled to an LLC generally needs a commercial auto policy. A personal policy can deny a claim if the car turns out to be business-owned or business-used.
Titling the car to the LLC doesn't create a deduction by itself; business use does. Only the business share of driving counts, commuting doesn't, and you keep a mileage log either way.

details.Existing car: Retitle at the DMV; lender must agree
details.New car: LLC buys it from the business account
details.Deduction: Business-use share only, with a log

entries.next_step: Call your insurer before you retitle anything and ask what commercial coverage would cost.

entries.title: Buying property through an LLC
entries.summary: An LLC can hold a rental or other property, but it needs commercial financing or cash, and since March 1, 2026 many all-cash entity purchases are reported to FinCEN.
body: Cash purchases are the simplest: the LLC is the buyer, the money comes from the LLC's account and the deed names the LLC. Financed purchases usually need a commercial or portfolio loan, often with 20–30% down and higher rates than a home mortgage, plus your personal guarantee for a new LLC.

Since March 1, 2026, FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Rule requires the closing or title professional to report most non-financed purchases of 1–4 unit homes, condos, co-ops and residential land by an entity or trust, including who owns or controls the buyer. You don't file it yourself, but expect to provide that information at closing.

Holding your own home in an LLC usually gives up the personal-residence capital gains exclusion and can complicate insurance and homestead protections. Moving a mortgaged property you already own into an LLC can trigger the loan's due-on-sale clause.
Putting assets into an LLC after a lawsuit or debt already exists can be undone by a court as a fraudulent transfer. The structure is for purchases you haven't made yet.
entries.next_step: Talk to a real estate attorney or CPA before closing in an LLC, especially for a home you'll live in.

entries.title: Running a nonprofit alongside your LLC
entries.summary: You add a separate nonprofit instead of converting the LLC. Separate EIN, bank accounts, books and board; money crosses only on paper at fair prices.
body: An LLC exists to earn profit for its owners. A 501(c)(3) must dedicate its assets permanently to charitable purposes, so the usual path is a new nonprofit formed from day one, with the LLC left as it is.
Each entity needs its own EIN, bank accounts, books and decision-makers. Shared cards and shared spreadsheets are where trouble starts, because nobody can later show whose money paid for what.

Value can move between them through gifts, sales, leases and service agreements, but only when priced at fair market value, approved in advance by board members with no stake in the deal, and documented at the time. The IRS gives deals approved this way a presumption that they were reasonable.

Who funds the nonprofit matters. If it is funded mostly by you and your LLC, it may be classified as a private foundation, which has much stricter self-dealing rules. Plan to raise money from the public too.
If your goal is just to support a cause, giving to an existing charity or using a fiscal sponsor can be far simpler than running your own organization.
steps: Write the mission in one paragraph and how the nonprofit will relate to the LLC.
File articles of incorporation as a nonprofit with a purpose and asset-dedication clause.
Seat a board that includes independent members, adopt bylaws and a conflict-of-interest policy.
Get a separate EIN and bank account, then apply for exemption on Form 1023 or 1023-EZ.

details.Money between them: Gift, sale, lease or service — fair value, on paper
details.Funding trap: Mostly-you funding can mean private foundation rules

entries.next_step: Before filing anything, decide whether a fiscal sponsor or simply donating would meet your goal.

entries.title: Nonprofit filings: Form 1023, fees and deadlines
entries.summary: Form 1023-EZ costs $275 and fits small organizations; the full Form 1023 costs $600. File within 27 months of forming, and never miss three annual returns in a row.
body: Order matters: state formation comes first, then the EIN, then the IRS application for recognition of exemption, which is filed online through Pay.gov.

Form 1023-EZ has a $275 user fee and is limited to small organizations that pass the IRS eligibility worksheet (for example, projected gross receipts of $50,000 or less a year and assets of $250,000 or less). Everyone else files the full Form 1023, with a $600 fee. A nonprofit tied to a business should discuss with an advisor which form fits.
Apply within 27 months of the end of the month you formed and exemption can reach back to your formation date.

Every year, file the right return: Form 990-N for organizations normally under $50,000 in gross receipts, 990-EZ or the full 990 above that. Missing a required return three years in a row automatically revokes tax-exempt status. Income from an unrelated business of $1,000 or more needs Form 990-T.
entries.next_step: Run the IRS eligibility worksheet in the Form 1023-EZ instructions before paying either fee.

entries.title: Buying an existing business from a retiring owner
entries.summary: Many profitable small businesses will change hands as owners retire. Buyers often combine seller financing with SBA-backed loans, after careful checks of the books.
body: A large number of small-business owners are nearing retirement, and some will sell profitable companies rather than close them. Buying one means you start with customers, staff and cash flow instead of an idea.

Common financing is a mix: a down payment, an SBA 7(a) loan through a participating lender, and seller financing, where the owner is paid part of the price over time. Seller financing also keeps the seller invested in a smooth handoff.

Due diligence is the whole game: three years of tax returns and bank statements that match the claimed profit, customer concentration (does one client make up most of revenue?), leases, licenses, debts and why the owner is really selling.
Use a business attorney and a CPA, and never sign based on numbers you haven't matched to bank records.

details.Red flag: One customer is most of revenue

entries.next_step: Ask a local SBDC or SCORE mentor to walk you through a sample buy-side checklist before you contact sellers.

entries.title: Find the one thing capping your growth
entries.summary: Revenue is leads × conversion × price. Before fixing anything, find which of the three (or your capacity) is the real ceiling.
body: Most stuck businesses have a dozen things that feel broken, but usually only one is the real ceiling. Everything else is a symptom. Fixing symptoms first wastes time and money.

Every business grows through some version of the same equation: how many people find you (leads), how many become customers (conversion), and how much each one pays over time (price and repeat purchases). A fourth limit is capacity, when you already have more demand than you can deliver.

Ask which sentence sounds like you. "The phone doesn't ring enough" is a leads problem. "People inquire but disappear" is conversion. "We sell, but each customer is barely worth it" is price. "More demand would just mean longer waits" is capacity.
A common hidden ceiling is a belief nobody tested, such as "customers only trust the owner" or "our market would never pay more." Test it before treating it as fact.
steps: Write down last month's leads, customers and average sale.
Multiply them out and see which number is weakest compared with your goal.
If you have a waiting list, treat capacity as the bottleneck first.
Fix that one lever before touching the others.

details.Rule: Fix one lever at a time

entries.next_step: Pull last month's numbers for leads, conversion and average sale, and circle the weakest.

entries.title: Case study: the expert who was the bottleneck
entries.summary: A three-location dental practice was capped by one doctor doing every visit. Handing off routine steps, raising price and getting paid upfront took it from about $160K to about $500K a month.
body: The founder personally did all five visits of every implant case, so the practice could only grow as fast as one calendar. Only two of the five visits truly needed his skill. Training associates on the other three roughly doubled capacity without hiring another senior expert.

With capacity freed up, the next moves were turning up spend on the channel that already worked and raising price. A close rate above 80% was the signal that price was too low; a 20% increase was followed by a higher close rate, not a lower one.

Collecting payment upfront (pay in full or finance) instead of pay-as-you-go was described as the biggest single unlock: cash arrived sooner and could be reinvested into a better patient experience, which supported higher prices.

The rest of the sequence: a short education video before the sales conversation, making the existing location more profitable instead of opening another, cutting the wait for a first appointment from weeks to about seven days, and only then using before-and-after results as organic content.

Reported results after 90 days: monthly revenue from about $160K to about $500K, average treatment value from $28K to $44K, and the growth goal reached without opening a new location. These figures come from the recorded show and weren't independently audited.
entries.next_step: List every step of your delivery and mark which ones truly need you; hand off the rest.

entries.title: Case study: rescuing a business weeks from empty
entries.summary: An indoor adventure park with about two weeks of cash ran one heavily stacked prepaid offer, a stripped-down page and a one-week giveaway, producing 3,700 leads.
body: Start by separating two problems that are easy to confuse: not enough customers, and not enough cash. The park was only half full on peak days but was also about to run out of money, so the emergency was cash.
The fix was one bet, not many: an all-summer pass priced well below the sum of its parts and paid in full upfront, pushed hard to the existing list just as families were planning summer.
The landing page was cut down to one decision, with a short video near the top and the most important trust point (a specific safety number) right next to the button.

A one-week giveaway with a real grand prize, a second-place prize and extra entries for sharing collected 3,700 leads in one local market. Non-winners were then offered a time-limited discount. As usual, a big share of entries arrived in the last 48 hours.
The win created the next bottleneck: a three-person sales team couldn't call 3,700 people in time. Plan staffing before a launch, and check local rules for prize promotions before you run one.
entries.next_step: Calculate your true monthly break-even, then design one prepaid offer for your existing customers.

entries.title: Case study: the roofer who chased the wrong jobs
entries.summary: A young roofing company shifted toward small repair jobs competitors skipped, used a 'menu close', sold maintenance memberships and charged for speed, going from about $32K to about $250K a month.
body: About 70% of revenue came from big replacement jobs, but the smaller repair jobs faced almost no competition because larger companies didn't want them. Less competition meant faster sales and happier customers.

The team raised the average ticket on those repairs by including more per visit, sent a short video before each visit so homeowners arrived warmed up, and doubled down on door-to-door sales, the one channel already converting well.
The menu close works by first telling the customer what they don't need. That honesty builds trust before recommending what they do need, and the close becomes a simple choice between options.

A low-cost annual maintenance membership barely covered its own cost but guaranteed a welcome visit every year. And because demand exceeded capacity, customers could pay a premium to be scheduled sooner.
Reported results: revenue from about $32K to about $250K a month and roughly four times the sales velocity. Figures are from the recorded show and weren't independently audited.

details.Close: Say what they don't need first

entries.next_step: List your job types by competition and profit, and pick the one nobody else wants.

entries.title: Case study: turning word of mouth into a system
entries.summary: A concierge medical practice made referrals deliberate: rewards that make the referrer look generous, booking the next visit before leaving, newsletters with a clear ask, and in-person events.
body: Referrals were happening by luck. The fix was giving every happy customer a specific, valuable reason to refer, and asking at every touchpoint instead of once.
Referral rewards work better when they make the referrer look generous, such as gifting a friend a real service, than when they feel like a coupon or a favor to the business.
"Book a month, fill a month": book each customer's next visit before they leave, then ask who they'll bring next time. The ask becomes part of the booking flow instead of an awkward moment.
Every newsletter and post needs one clear call to action. For high-trust, high-price services, in-person events beat cold ads, and a giveaway can make the price familiar before anyone has to decide.

When the plan hit a seasonal market with too few existing events, the practice started its own lecture series instead. The specific tactic changed; the strategy of warm, in-person trust-building stayed.

details.Reward: A gift that makes the referrer look good
details.Habit: Book the next visit, ask who they'll bring

entries.next_step: Add one referral ask and one clear call to action to your next customer email.

entries.title: Case study: for people who hate selling
entries.summary: A mission-driven coaching business replaced 30 hours a week of DMs and a four-hour pitch with a structured webinar, recurring billing and priced one-on-one access.
body: The founder believed structure and pricing meant "selling out." But people only feel sold to when the selling is bad. Good selling makes a purchase clear and easy for the people you're trying to help.
A long, unstructured pitch isn't more honest than a tight one; it just loses more people. A structured webinar covers the promise, the story, proof and the offer in a predictable order.
Ads aimed only at existing followers will always convert well and always plateau. Selling to strangers needs messages that start from their problem, not your product.

Recurring billing removes the need to win the customer again every month. And personal time has a real price: if someone wants a one-on-one call, charge for it, so the default path is the group offer.
Reported early result: weekly time in DMs dropped from about 30 hours to 3–5, with the team pre-screening and directing people to the webinar.

details.Reframe: Bad selling is the problem, not selling

entries.next_step: Write a five-part outline for one structured presentation: promise, story, proof, offer, next step.

entries.title: Case study: escaping the price war
entries.summary: A moving company compared only on hourly rate added tiered packages, a cost cap, free upgrades for referral partners and personalized outreach. Referral jobs earned about 3× the profit.
body: When customers can't tell two options apart, they pick the cheaper one, because price is the only thing left to compare. The fix is adding real, named differences.
Most buying decisions turn on speed, safety and ease. A premium tier that bundles your best crew, materials and guarantees gives customers something to compare besides price.
For anything priced by time, the hidden fear is "what if this costs far more than expected?" A guaranteed ceiling on cost answers it directly.

Referral partners such as real estate agents care about their reputation. Letting them say "I got you upgraded for free" works better than a small kickback. Then go after the whole organization, not one person, and personalize outreach instead of blasting one template.
The show still said "not yet," judging the business too early for multi-location growth. A no about timing or fit is different from a no about quality.

details.Fix: Tiers built on speed, safety, ease

entries.next_step: Design a premium tier and write one guarantee that removes your customers' biggest fear.

sources.label: Acquisition.com YouTube — 'Give Me 42 Minutes, I'll Show You How To Sell Like The Top 1%'

entries.title: Case study: when the only cap is you
entries.summary: An online teaching business with a working funnel stopped capping ad spend by instinct, made hundreds of ads from community content, and narrowed targeting to scale.
body: A spending cap not based on real math, such as the cost per customer where you stop being profitable, is just caution dressed up as a budget. Work out the real number first.
Spend in a cadence: a small test budget in week one to find winning ads, then heavier spend as the launch nears and urgency peaks.

Going from a handful of ads to hundreds doesn't need a big production budget. Screenshots from an active community, clips from live sessions and customers' own posts can all become ads, with permission.

To scale beyond people who already know you, speak to their problem rather than your product. Present one main offer instead of a cheap and a premium option side by side, test big structural changes as clean split tests at the same price, and use many narrow audiences with their own messages.
entries.next_step: Calculate the most you can pay for one customer and still profit; that's your real spending limit.

sources.label: Acquisition.com YouTube — 'Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger'

entries.title: Case study: real prices, quoted live
entries.summary: An event company replaced invented, emailed quotes with a cost-based pricing tool used live on calls, a price lock, separate setters and closers, and one key question.
body: Every quote was built from scratch and emailed days later, so nobody knew the margin and prospects had time to drift away. The fix was a pricing engine: costs that scale with the job, costs that don't, and a target margin, used live on the call.
A price lock (the price won't change as long as the scope doesn't) removes client anxiety. Define scope in writing: date, venue, a headcount range.
One early question, "how many events like this do you run a year?", revealed far bigger opportunities. One deal reportedly went from $80K to $240K.

The founder outsold two full-time reps working part-time, so the reps switched to booking qualified calls only, with daily (not weekly) check-ins. A sponsorship at an event full of ideal customers reportedly turned $15K into a $500K deal.

details.Key question: How often do you need this?

entries.next_step: Build a simple spreadsheet that prices your typical job from real costs plus a target margin.

sources.label: Acquisition.com YouTube — 'How to Get Rich for Service-Based Businesses'

entries.title: Pricing and building an offer people want
entries.summary: People buy when the expected result is big and believable and the wait and effort feel small. Find your price range by asking customers, and test a premium version.
body: A widely used way to think about value (popularized in Alex Hormozi's $100M Offers) is: the size of the dream outcome times how likely the buyer thinks it is, divided by the time it takes and the effort it costs. You raise value by making the result more believable (proof, guarantees) or faster and easier, not just by adding features.

To find a real price range, ask prospects four questions: at what price is this too expensive to consider, too cheap to trust, getting expensive but still worth it, and a real bargain. The answers show a range instead of a guess.
If almost everyone says yes, your price is probably too low. Raise it in steps and watch price × close rate together; selling a few fewer people at a much higher price can still be a win.
Try the "add a zero" exercise: multiply your price by ten and ask what would have to be true to justify it. The answer often describes a premium tier worth offering to a few customers.
Guarantees, bonuses and payment plans can make an offer easier to accept, but every claim must be true and every condition clearly stated.
entries.next_step: Ask five recent prospects the four price questions and plot their answers.

entries.title: Getting more customers: the four ways to reach people
entries.summary: There are four ways to get leads yourself: warm outreach, cold outreach, free content and paid ads. Master one before adding the next.
body: One popular framework (from Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads) sorts lead generation into four activities you can do yourself: reaching out one-to-one to people who already know you (warm outreach), to people who don't (cold outreach), posting free content to many people, and paying to show ads to many people.
Others can do it for you, too: customer referrals, employees, agencies and affiliates or partners.

Inbound search, such as local service ads and Google Business listings, is usually the most profitable channel, but there are only so many people searching. Past that, businesses need "interruption" marketing: outreach, content or ads that reach people who weren't looking yet.
The most common mistake is doing a little of everything. Pick the channel that already brings customers, do much more of it, and only then add a second.
Know your customer segments. Data on which customers are worth the most lets you aim outreach and ads at more people like them.

details.Yourself: Warm outreach, cold outreach, content, ads

entries.next_step: Count where your last 20 customers came from, and double your effort on the top source this month.

entries.title: Speed to lead: answer first, win more
entries.summary: People comparing options usually go with whoever responds first. Faster responses tend to raise close rates and show-up rates and lower the cost per customer.
body: When someone is shopping around, the business that responds first often wins, and the gap is measured in minutes, not days.

Speed shows up everywhere: how fast you answer an inquiry, how soon a new customer can be seen, how quickly a quote arrives. In the dental case study, cutting the wait for a first appointment from two to four weeks to about a week lifted close and show-up rates together.

Fixes are usually simple: route leads to a phone that someone actually answers, text back within minutes, remove the queue between form and first call, and track response time as a number on the same dashboard as revenue.

Automated text-backs and AI receptionists can help after hours, but phone and text rules apply: get consent before automated marketing texts or calls, and tell people they're talking to an automated system where required.

details.Measure: Minutes from lead to first contact
details.Careful: Consent rules for automated texts and calls

entries.next_step: Time how long your next five leads wait for a first reply, and set a target under five minutes during business hours.

sources.label: FCC — AI-generated voices in robocalls are covered by the TCPA

entries.title: Nail it before you scale it
entries.summary: A second location or product multiplies whatever problems the first one has. Max out what you already run before adding more.
body: When growth stalls, the instinct is to open another location, hire more people or add another product. Usually the better move is to make the existing one much more profitable first.
A second unit copies the first one's weaknesses. Only when the first is running near its real ceiling does expansion make the math better instead of just more complicated.
The same goes for automation: automating a process that was never the bottleneck spends money without moving growth.
Signs you're ready: the core bottleneck is solved, margins are healthy, the business runs for a week without you, and demand is clearly greater than you can serve.

details.Reality: Max out the one you have

entries.next_step: Write down your current location's ceiling: the revenue it could do if every slot were filled at your current price.

entries.title: Keep the customers you have: retention and recurring revenue
entries.summary: Keeping a customer is cheaper than finding a new one. Memberships, renewals and well-timed upgrades raise what each customer is worth.
body: Lifetime value is the profit a customer brings over the whole relationship, not just the first sale. Raising it lets you afford more marketing for each new customer.

Recurring options, such as memberships, maintenance plans and subscriptions, remove the need to win the customer again each time. Even a small membership can be valuable because it guarantees a reason to stay in touch.
Upgrades sell best while people are actively engaged, not after they've mentally finished. Offer the next step at natural moments, more than once.
Recurring billing comes with rules: clear terms before the customer pays, express consent, and an easy way to cancel. Make cancelling as easy as signing up.
entries.next_step: Design one small recurring offer that gives customers a reason to come back every month or year.

entries.title: Founder field notes: fear, decisions and hiring
entries.summary: Short ideas worth keeping: fear lives in the vague, an unmade decision lasts forever, teach new hires the shortcut, and a no about fit isn't a no about merit.
body: Fear lives in the vague. "I might fail" has no answer; "what if I ask 100 people and all say no" does: adjust the offer and ask 100 more. Name the specific version of the fear.
A decision you make gets corrected by feedback. A decision you never make teaches you nothing. Most people lose more time at the fork than they would have lost picking wrong.
Train people the way you wish you'd been taught: straight to what works, skipping the dead ends you already found.
Price referral bonuses for what a referral is really worth. A tiny bonus for a referral that brings tens of thousands in profit underprices your best channel.
A bad day isn't a strategy meeting. Push on if the core assumption still holds; pivot only if it's been proven false. And a rejection about timing or fit is not a verdict on your work.

details.On decisions: Decide, then let feedback correct you

entries.next_step: Write down the specific version of the fear holding you back, and the first small test that would answer it.

sources.label: The Diary Of A CEO — Alex Hormozi interview

entries.title: Building in the age of AI
entries.summary: AI tools are useful leverage, but practical businesses that deliver real-world results, and a reputation for doing so, are harder to copy than a thin app on top of a model.
body: A recurring argument in recent founder interviews is that many businesses built as a thin layer on top of AI models will be copied or replaced quickly, while practical businesses, such as trades and local services, stay valuable because they deliver something physical and trusted.

Use AI where it saves time: drafting, research, answering repeat questions with human review, summarizing data. Keep making the hard judgment calls yourself, since judgment is a skill that fades when unused.
Reputation and real results are moats. Reviews, case studies and repeat customers can't be generated by a competitor overnight.
Revenue retention, meaning keeping and growing existing customers, often matters more than winning new ones.
entries.next_step: Pick one repetitive task in your week, try an AI tool for it with your own review, and measure the time saved.

sources.label: The Diary Of A CEO — 'Stop Chasing AI, Build This Instead'

entries.title: Zero to One: build something new instead of competing
entries.summary: Peter Thiel's argument: competition erodes profit, so aim to create something new and dominate a small market first, using technology, network effects, scale or brand.
body: Copying what works (going from 1 to n) adds more of something familiar. Creating something new (going from 0 to 1) is rarer and more valuable. Thiel argues that businesses stuck in intense competition compete away their profits.
He suggests asking yourself what important truth you believe that most people don't. A good answer can point to a business others aren't building yet.

Durable businesses tend to have some combination of proprietary technology that is much better than the alternatives, network effects (more valuable as more people use it), economies of scale, and a strong brand.
Start by dominating a small, specific market, then expand to nearby ones. And don't ignore distribution: a great product nobody hears about loses to an average one that reaches people.
entries.next_step: Write down one belief about your market that most competitors would disagree with, and what business it implies.

entries.title: Building software for the masses on a small budget
entries.summary: Solve one narrow, widely shared problem by hand first, ship a lean version on free tiers, lead with a free plan, and build sharing into the product.
body: Before writing code, be the software: run the bookings with a phone and a spreadsheet, track a shop's stock by text, charge a small fee. You'll learn exactly what people will pay for.
The test: if a thousand more customers showed up tomorrow, could you serve them without hiring an army? If only software would make that possible, you're on a scalable path.
Ship the smallest useful version fast. Modern no-code and AI-assisted builders, plus generous free tiers for hosting, databases and payments, can keep early costs very low.

Distribution beats code. Lead with a genuinely useful free tier, write for the exact searches struggling users type, show the build in short videos, and design growth into the product: shared links, a "made with" mark on free output, referral credits.
Bootstrapping keeps control but is slower. Expect a niche to take a few years of iteration to prove itself.
entries.next_step: Find one problem people complain about in forums, and solve it by hand for three paying people before building anything.

sources.label: SBA — Market research and competitive analysis

entries.title: Starting a small AI or automation services business
entries.summary: Pick one industry, solve one costly problem (like missed calls or slow quotes), price it simply, and follow the rules on calls, texts and data. Ignore the luxury-lifestyle promises.
body: Many recent videos promise four-hour days and million-dollar years from an "AI agency." Treat those as marketing, often for the presenter's own course or software, which they usually disclose earning commissions on.

What tends to work: choose one niche you understand, find a costly, specific problem (missed calls after hours, slow quotes, unanswered reviews), and offer one result at one price. A useful free audit of a business's online listing, sent as a short personal video, often opens more doors than a generic cold email.

Set rules from the start. Automated marketing calls and texts generally need prior consent, and the FCC has said AI-generated voices count as "artificial" voices under the TCPA. Marketing email must follow CAN-SPAM: honest headers and subject lines, a postal address and a working opt-out. Only contact a client's real past customers, never bought lists.
Be honest about what the tool does. Test it, keep humans reviewing important outputs, and put the scope, price and data handling in a written agreement.

details.Start: One niche, one problem, one price

entries.next_step: Pick one local industry and list its three most expensive everyday problems before choosing any tool.

entries.title: From spreadsheets to accounting software to ERP
entries.summary: Most small businesses move from spreadsheets to bookkeeping software, and only much later to an ERP like NetSuite.
body: Stage one is a separate business account and a simple spreadsheet. Stage two, usually once you invoice clients or have regular expenses, is bookkeeping software such as QuickBooks or Xero, which connects to your bank and categorizes transactions.

Stage three is an ERP (enterprise resource planning) system such as Oracle NetSuite, which runs finance, reporting and month-end close across a growing company. In a NetSuite sales call shared with this guide, the account executive said it usually becomes a fit around $5 million in annual revenue. That's the rep's rule of thumb, not an official requirement.
A bookkeeper or CPA can tell you in one meeting which stage you're in.
entries.next_step: Connect your business bank account to bookkeeping software before tax season.

entries.title: The Free Loop: win customers by helping first
entries.summary: Pick one sharp problem, give away a quick win that solves it, wrap it in a real story, make it easy to get, follow up like a person, then invite — and feed what you learn back in.
body: Start with one specific, slightly annoying problem customers keep naming, small enough to fix in one sitting. Read your last twenty customer messages and highlight every "I can't", "I never" or "why does".

Turn it into a quick win: a checklist, template, calculator or mini-audit that leaves the person with something done. Promise it as "By the end you'll have ___ in about ___ minutes." It should be useful even if they never talk to you.
Tell a short story around it (the moment, what it cost, what changed, the tool) and keep the ask to a sentence or two. Never invent stories or customers.

Make it easy to receive: usually just an email field, instant delivery, and a thank-you page that says what's coming and how to leave. Follow up with the asset, one tip and one question, signed by a real person.
When someone engages, offer one next step and say plainly that no is fine. The most repeated reply becomes your next sharp problem. That feedback is what makes it a loop instead of a funnel.
steps: Highlight complaints in your last 20 customer messages and pick the most common.
Build a free asset that fixes it in under 30 minutes.
Publish one story about the problem with a one-line link to the asset.
Send a welcome email with one tip and one question, and read every reply.

details.Stage 3–4: Tell the story, make it easy to get
details.Stage 5–6: Follow up like a person, invite and listen

entries.next_step: Read your last 20 customer messages and write down the complaint that appears most often.

entries.title: Salesy versus useful: rewriting your messages
entries.summary: A pushy pitch asks the customer to take the risk. A useful message takes it on yourself by giving something first. Six common lines, rewritten.
body: Opening a message to a stranger. Pushy: "I help businesses 10x their revenue, got 15 minutes?" Useful: name the specific problem you noticed and offer one idea they can use whether or not they reply.
Ending a post. Pushy: "DM me READY!" Useful: "The checklist behind this story is free; take whatever helps."
Creating urgency. Pushy: "Limited spots, book now!" Useful: state a real limit and how to tell whether you're a fit: "I have room for four new clients this month."
Following up. Pushy: "Just checking in." Useful: "Did the checklist catch anything surprising? Reply with what you found and I'll tell you what I'd look at next."

Starting a call. Pushy: "Let me tell you about our packages." Useful: "Before anything else, what part of this is costing you the most right now?" Handling hesitation: offer to check back later, or to leave it there.

details.Pushy: Asks for time or money first

entries.next_step: Take the last message you sent a prospect and rewrite it so it gives something before it asks.

entries.title: Anatomy of a webinar registration page
entries.summary: Most free-masterclass pages use six blocks in the same order, each clearing one hesitation: the promise, a proof strip, three outcomes, a 'this is for you if' list, the guide, and a date-picker ask.
body: The open: one headline naming the transformation, one button, a real face, no navigation.
The proof strip: a small row of faces, stars or a headcount just below the fold. A number does more than an adjective, but it must be true.
The promise grid: three specific outcomes attendees will walk away with, framed as results, not features.
The mirror: a short "this is for you if…" checklist in the visitor's own words, which does the qualifying.
The guide and the ask: a short bio with one concrete credential, then a choice of a specific date and time rather than a vague "sign up", with the same button repeated down the page.

details.4–6: The mirror, the guide, a date-picker ask

entries.next_step: Draft your page in these six blocks before designing anything, and remove any claim you can't back up.

sources.label: FTC — Endorsement Guides and testimonials FAQ

entries.title: The nine-part landing page home-service companies use
entries.summary: Roofing, window, siding and sunroom ads tend to land on the same page: outcome headline, two promises, a self-sort grid, four steps, a provenance story, proof, a short form, a deadline band and a license footer.
body: Above the fold: a headline that names the outcome ("a room you'll actually use"), a phone number in the header and a trust mark. Then two short promises side by side, one about fit and one about risk.
A grid of five or six product variations lets visitors pick their own situation, which makes the form feel like a continuation of a choice already made.
A four-step view of the whole process (consult, design and price, build, warranty) answers "what am I agreeing to?" A photo block about how long the company has existed answers "is this real?"
Proof comes as a video testimonial plus named, located reviews. The form asks for name, address, ZIP, phone and email in that order, with a consent box for calls and texts above one action button.

A colored band pairs a discount with financing and an end date, and a dense footer carries license numbers and financing disclosures that many states require. If you borrow the structure, use your own photos, real reviews and real deadlines.
entries.next_step: Map your current landing page against the nine parts and add the one that's missing.

sources.label: FTC — Consumer reviews and testimonials rule

entries.title: Marketing rules every small business should know
entries.summary: Real testimonials only, typical results next to standout ones, paid relationships disclosed up front, honest email with an opt-out, and consent before automated calls or texts.
body: Reviews and testimonials: since October 21, 2024, an FTC rule prohibits fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-generated ones and ones from people who never used the product. Buying reviews and undisclosed insider reviews are covered too. If you show a standout result, the FTC's Endorsement Guides expect you to show what people generally achieve; "results may vary" alone isn't enough.
Disclose paid relationships clearly, near the claim, not only in the footer. Ads that look like articles need a clear "advertisement" label before the click.
Email: under CAN-SPAM, use honest sender and subject lines, identify the message as an ad, include a valid postal address and a working unsubscribe, and honor opt-outs promptly.

Calls and texts: automated marketing calls and texts generally need prior express written consent under the TCPA, and the FCC treats AI-generated voices as artificial voices. Subscriptions must disclose terms, get consent and make cancelling simple.
This is general information. Rules vary by state and change, so have important campaigns reviewed by an attorney.
entries.next_step: Check your website and last email for a postal address, an unsubscribe link and any testimonial you can't document.

sources.label: FTC — Consumer reviews and testimonials rule Q&A

entries.title: Speaking to people who don't know you yet
entries.summary: Audiences range from people who already know your product to people who don't yet realize they have the problem. To grow, write for the larger, colder groups.
body: A classic copywriting idea from Eugene Schwartz sorts people into levels of awareness: most aware (know you and are ready), product-aware, solution-aware, problem-aware and unaware.
Messages about your product work on the small group who already know you. That's why ads aimed at followers convert well but stop scaling.
To reach more people, lead with the problem and its cost in their words, then introduce the kind of solution, and only then your product.
Test several hooks aimed at different levels, keep the winners, and let the colder messages carry more of your budget as you grow.

details.Coldest: Don't know they have the problem

entries.next_step: Rewrite your best ad so the first line names the problem, not the product.

entries.title: Building a personal brand that stands out
entries.summary: Attention goes to whoever breaks the pattern in a way people like. Combine real skill with the traits that make you different, instead of hiding them.
body: A recent argument from Alex Hormozi, using Dolly Parton as the example: standing out rarely comes from one trait. It comes from an unusual combination of them, each one making the whole rarer.

The parts of yourself you hide for fear of judgment are often the parts that make you memorable. The degree to which you break the pattern earns attention; whether people like how you broke it decides whether it's positive.
Being different doesn't replace being good. Plenty of talented people don't stick because they're good but not great, or great at one thing with nothing else around it.
In practice: pick a skill you're getting genuinely excellent at, post consistently about the work and the lessons, and let your real background, interests and quirks show.

details.Habit: Post the work and the lessons

entries.next_step: List five things about you that rarely go together, and use one of them in your next post.

sources.label: Alex Hormozi — 'If I Started A Personal Brand In 2026'

entries.title: LinkedIn posts that get read and start conversations
entries.summary: Short personal stories with one clear lesson, honest progress updates and comments on other people's posts tend to do more than polished announcements.
body: Posts that people stop for usually start with a specific moment (fixing a parent's cabinet hinges, a conversation at dinner) and end with one lesson connected to your work.
Honest progress builds trust. "We don't have our first client yet, here's what I'm building and why" is more credible than vague claims.
Write the first two lines as the hook, since LinkedIn shows only those before "see more." Keep paragraphs short, and end with a question people can answer.
Thoughtful comments on posts in your field often bring more profile visits than your own posts. Fill in your headline with who you help and how, and keep your contact details current.
entries.next_step: Write one post about a small, specific moment from this week and the lesson it taught you.

entries.title: Short-form video and faceless channels: what's real
entries.summary: Short videos can reach a lot of people for free, but the income claims in 'faceless channel' tutorials are rarely verifiable and often sell the presenter's course.
body: Short-form video (Shorts, Reels, TikTok) can put a product or story in front of many people at no cost. Vertical, full-screen video, a strong first second and a clear topic matter more than expensive equipment.
Platform payouts vary a lot by audience country, topic and each platform's monetization rules, which change often. Some content, such as reused clips from others, can be ineligible.
Tutorials claiming hundreds of thousands of dollars from faceless channels or reels usually link to paid prompts, courses or tools the presenter profits from. Treat their screenshots as unverified.

For a business, the more reliable use is showing real work: before-and-afters, answers to customer questions, the build in progress, with a clear next step at the end. Never repost other people's videos as your own.

details.Payouts: Vary by audience and platform rules

entries.next_step: Film one 30-second before-and-after or answer to a common customer question this week.

sources.label: YouTube Help — YouTube Partner Program overview

entries.title: Finding clients on Craigslist and job boards
entries.summary: Repeated job posts signal a lasting problem. A role re-posted three times, like an estimator seat, can point to a business that would pay for a tool or service that fixes it.
body: Gig and job boards show what businesses are struggling with right now. A position re-posted several times, such as an estimator or bookkeeper, suggests a problem they haven't solved.
Sort posts by fit with what you actually offer, read the full post before reaching out, and note the city, date and what they asked for.

Reach out with something specific: what you noticed in their post, one idea for their problem, and an easy next step. Don't send the same template to everyone, and don't pretend to be a job applicant if you're offering a service.
Be careful on any board: never pay to get work, never accept overpayments with a request to send the difference back, and confirm a business is real before sharing personal details.

details.Signal: The same role posted again and again

entries.next_step: Search your local board for roles that match your skill and list the ones posted more than twice.

entries.title: Cold outreach that gets replies: lead with a useful audit
entries.summary: Instead of asking a stranger for time, send a short personal video or note showing one specific problem you found and how you'd fix it.
body: Most cold messages fail because they ask for the most precious thing the owner has, time, before giving anything. Leading with something useful flips that.

Pick prospects you can qualify in seconds, such as local businesses with few or unanswered Google reviews if you sell reputation help. Record a two-minute video walking through their listing and one improvement.
Send a short message asking whether they'd like the video, then send it when they say yes. Make it about them, not your credentials.
Keep it legal and decent: honest subject lines, an easy way to opt out, no bought email lists, and only contact a client's real past customers when you run campaigns for them.
entries.next_step: Pick three local businesses, find one specific fix for each, and offer to send a short video.

entries.title: Affiliates and user-generated content
entries.summary: Paying partners for results and working with everyday creators can grow a business without the founder on camera, if every paid relationship is disclosed.
body: Affiliate programs pay partners a commission for customers they send. Marketing leaders who've scaled launches describe finding the channel that's actually driving growth, often affiliates, and doing more of it before trying anything new.

User-generated content (UGC) means videos and posts made by customers or small creators. The barrier to working with creators is lower than many owners think; a polite, specific message often starts the conversation.
Give partners clear rules: no false claims, no fake reviews, and a visible disclosure of the paid relationship in every post.
Track results by partner so you can reward what works and stop what doesn't.
entries.next_step: Ask three happy customers whether they'd make a short honest video, and offer a clearly disclosed thank-you.

sources.label: FTC — Disclosures 101 for social media influencers

entries.title: Memberships and fan funding (Patreon and similar)
entries.summary: Creators and community organizations can fund ongoing work through monthly memberships, as long as members get a clear, steady benefit.
body: Platforms like Patreon let supporters pay monthly for access to exclusive posts, community, early releases or behind-the-scenes content. Tiers often start at a few dollars and go up from there.
What sustains a membership is consistency: a clear promise (what members get and how often) that you can keep for months.
Fees, payouts and taxes vary by platform and change over time; check the current pricing page before you launch. Money from memberships is generally taxable income.
For a nonprofit, member support can fit alongside donations, but keep the books separate and follow the rules for donor acknowledgments.
entries.next_step: Write one sentence describing exactly what a member gets each month, then price two tiers.

entries.title: Four communication habits that carry most conversations
entries.summary: Say the point first, listen to understand, build rapport with follow-up questions, and steady your nerves. Each habit has decent evidence behind it, with limits.
body: Speak to lead: put your recommendation in the first sentence, then two reasons, then stop. Cut filler softeners, but keep honest statements of what you don't know; research suggests calibrated uncertainty doesn't read as weak.

Listen to understand: give full attention, say back what you heard, and ask a follow-up before changing the subject. Studies of live conversations found people who asked more follow-up questions were better liked.

Build rapport: ask open questions, start on common ground (people, work, fun, goals), keep it light, share a little back, and leave while the energy is good. People tend to underestimate how much others liked talking with them.
Steady your body and mind: slow breathing before speaking can help, and telling yourself "I'm excited" helped people perform better in short lab tasks. Treat both as useful tools, not guarantees.
entries.next_step: In your next meeting, write your recommendation as one sentence and say it first.

sources.label: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2017) — question-asking and liking

entries.title: Selling to businesses versus selling to consumers
entries.summary: Consumers buy fast and emotionally in larger numbers; businesses buy slowly, in groups, on proof of return. Price, offer and follow-up differ for each.
body: Business-to-consumer (B2C) sales usually mean many customers, lower prices and quicker decisions, often made by one person. Clear outcomes, trust signals, easy checkout and good follow-up matter most.
Business-to-business (B2B) sales usually mean fewer, larger deals, several decision-makers and longer cycles. Buyers want proof the purchase pays for itself: time saved, revenue added, risk reduced.

A useful pattern for both is a ladder of offers: a free or low-cost entry, a core offer and a premium tier. Promotions such as giveaways can build a list, and people who don't win can be offered a discounted version.
Whatever the audience, the rules about honest claims, real deadlines and clear terms are the same.
entries.next_step: Write down who actually signs off on a purchase of what you sell, and what proof they need.

entries.title: How to open a checking account
entries.summary: What almost every bank and credit union asks for, how long it takes, and how to pick an account you will not pay to keep.
body: A checking account is the everyday account your paycheck lands in and your bills come out of. Opening one usually takes 10 to 20 minutes online or at a branch.

Federal law requires banks to verify who you are, so expect to give a government photo ID, your Social Security number (some banks accept an ITIN), your date of birth and a home address. Many applications also ask for a way to fund the account, such as a debit card or another bank's routing and account number.
Before you apply, decide what matters most: no monthly fee, no overdraft fees, branches near you, or a large free ATM network. Those four things decide most of what an account will cost you.
If a bank turns you down, it is often because of a checking-history report (ChexSystems), not your credit score. You still have options; see the second-chance banking entry.
steps: Pick two or three accounts to compare: one big bank, one credit union, one online bank.
Read each account's fee schedule for the monthly fee, how to waive it, overdraft fees and out-of-network ATM fees.
Gather ID, Social Security number or ITIN, address and an opening deposit if one is required.
Apply online or at a branch, then set up direct deposit so a waiver condition is met automatically.

details.What to bring: Photo ID, SSN or ITIN, address, opening deposit
details.Watch for: Monthly fees, overdraft fees, ATM fees

entries.next_step: Compare one big bank, one credit union and one online bank side by side using their fee schedules.

entries.title: Bank On certified accounts: the low-cost safe bet
entries.summary: Accounts certified to have no overdraft fees, a small or waivable monthly fee and a $25-or-less opening deposit.
body: Bank On is a national program that certifies checking accounts against a fixed set of standards. If an account carries the Bank On certification, you already know the basics without reading the fine print.

Under the 2025–2026 National Account Standards, a certified account may not charge overdraft or insufficient-funds fees. The monthly fee must be $5 or less, or $10 or less if there are at least two free ways to waive it. The opening deposit must be $25 or less, and there can be no fees for opening, closing, dormancy or low balances.
Certified accounts must also include a free debit card, free live phone support, free direct deposit and free electronic statements, and be FDIC or NCUA insured.

Joinbankon.org keeps a state-by-state directory of more than 500 certified accounts, including big-bank options like Chase Secure Banking, Bank of America Advantage SafeBalance and Wells Fargo Clear Access Banking, plus many local credit unions.
steps: Open joinbankon.org and choose your state.
Pick a certified account from a bank or credit union with a branch or ATM near you.
Open it online or in person with your ID and up to $25.

details.Monthly fee: $5 or less (or $10 if waivable two ways)

entries.next_step: Search your state on joinbankon.org and pick a certified account near you.

entries.title: Chase Total Checking
entries.summary: Chase's standard checking account: big branch and ATM network, a $15 monthly fee that is easy to waive, and a $50 overdraft cushion.
body: Chase Total Checking is the account most Chase customers start with. It comes with the full Chase branch and ATM network and the Chase mobile app, including mobile check deposit.

The monthly service fee is $15. It is waived in any statement period where you have $500 or more in qualifying electronic deposits (such as direct deposit), keep $1,500 or more at the start of each day, keep a $5,000 average across linked Chase accounts and investments, or link a qualifying Chase checking account.

Chase Overdraft Assist means no overdraft fee if you are overdrawn by $50 or less at the end of the business day, or if you bring the balance back to $50 or less overdrawn by the end of the next business day. Beyond that, overdraft fees apply.

Chase usually makes check deposits available by the next business day if they arrive before the cutoff (11 PM Eastern for mobile deposits). Deposits on weekends and holidays are processed the next business day.

details.Easiest waiver: $500+ in direct deposits per statement period
details.Overdraft: No fee if overdrawn $50 or less (Overdraft Assist)

entries.next_step: If you get paid by direct deposit of $500 or more, this account costs $0; otherwise compare Chase Secure Banking.

entries.title: Chase Secure Banking
entries.summary: A Bank On certified Chase account with no overdraft fees, no opening deposit and a $4.95 fee waived by $250 in electronic deposits.
body: Chase Secure Banking is built for people who want Chase's branches and app without the risk of overdraft fees. Transactions that would overdraw the account are declined instead of charged.
The monthly fee is $4.95, waived in any statement period with $250 or more in electronic deposits. There is no minimum opening deposit.

It is Bank On certified, which means it meets the national standard for safe, affordable accounts. The trade-off is that you do not get paper checks, so rent or bills that require a check need a money order or cashier's check instead.

details.Checked: Bank On directory and Bankrate, October 2026

entries.next_step: Good fit if you want a big-bank branch nearby and never want an overdraft fee.

entries.title: Bank of America Advantage SafeBalance
entries.summary: A Bank On certified, no-overdraft account: $4.95 a month, waived under age 25 or with a $500 daily balance; $25 to open.
body: Advantage SafeBalance is Bank of America's checkless account. Purchases that would overdraw it are declined, so there are no overdraft fees.
The monthly fee is $4.95, waived if you are under 25 (including students) or keep a $500 minimum daily balance. It takes $25 to open.
It is Bank On certified. Like most no-overdraft accounts, it does not come with paper checks.

details.Monthly fee: $4.95, waived under 25 or with $500 daily balance

entries.title: Wells Fargo Clear Access Banking
entries.summary: No overdraft fees, $5 a month (waived for ages 13–24 or qualifying deposits), $25 to open, Bank On certified.
body: Clear Access Banking is Wells Fargo's account with no overdraft fees. Wells Fargo declines transactions it cannot cover, though a negative balance can still happen in rare cases such as a tip added after approval or a returned deposit. You won't be charged a fee, but you'll need to bring the balance back up.
The monthly fee is $5, waived for primary account owners aged 13 to 24 or with qualifying deposits. It takes $25 to open.
Wells Fargo markets it for teens, students and anyone who wants a second chance at banking.

entries.title: Capital One 360 Checking
entries.summary: An online-first account with no monthly fee, no minimum, no overdraft fees and 70,000+ fee-free ATMs.
body: 360 Checking has no monthly fee and no minimum balance to open or keep. Capital One also charges no overdraft fees; you choose between auto-decline, a free transfer from savings, or a no-fee overdraft option.

You get more than 70,000 fee-free ATMs through Capital One, MoneyPass and Allpoint, including machines in some Target, Walgreens and CVS stores. Capital One also has a smaller set of branches and cafés in some cities.
Capital One completed its purchase of Discover in May 2025, so Discover bank customers may see their accounts move to Capital One over time.
entries.next_step: A strong no-cost option if you mostly bank by phone and can use partner ATMs.
