entries.title: Credit unions: how to join and why people do
entries.summary: Member-owned, not-for-profit banks that often have lower fees and loan rates. Most let you join if you live or work in the area.
body: A credit union works like a bank but is owned by its members. Deposits are insured by the NCUA (the National Credit Union Administration) up to $250,000, the same protection the FDIC gives at banks.

Every credit union has a field of membership, meaning who is allowed to join. It is usually broad: living, working, worshipping or going to school in an area, working for a partner employer, or being related to a member. Joining normally means opening a small savings share account, often $5 to $25.

For example, Hughes Federal Credit Union in Tucson lets anyone who lives, works, worships or studies in Tucson join. Its online application asks for a Social Security number, a government photo ID that is more than 30 days old, a funding source and your previous address if you moved within two years.
Credit unions are also where you find payday alternative loans (PALs), small loans capped at 28% APR, which are far cheaper than payday lenders.
steps: Use the NCUA's credit union locator to find credit unions near you.
Check each one's eligibility page to see if you qualify.
Open a membership savings account, then add checking.

details.Who can join: Usually anyone who lives or works in the area

entries.next_step: Look up credit unions near your ZIP with the NCUA locator and check who can join.

entries.title: Find insured banks and credit unions near your ZIP
entries.summary: Use official government lookups to see every insured branch near you and confirm a bank is real before you hand over money.
body: The FDIC's BankFind tool lists every FDIC-insured bank and its branches, searchable by name, city or ZIP. The Banking Agent engine uses the same FDIC data: type your ZIP code in the chat and it will list insured branches near you.
For credit unions, the NCUA's credit union locator shows every federally insured credit union by address or ZIP.
Check a bank's name on BankFind before you open an account, especially with an app or website you have not heard of. If an app says it is a fintech, not a bank, look up its partner bank instead.
steps: Type your 5-digit ZIP code into the chat on the home page, or open FDIC BankFind.
Shortlist two or three institutions with a branch or ATM near you.
Read each one's account fee schedule before you apply.
entries.next_step: Type your ZIP code in the chat to see insured branches near you.

entries.title: Denied a bank account? ChexSystems and second chances
entries.summary: Banks screen your checking history, not just credit. You can get your report free, dispute errors and still open a second-chance account.
body: Most banks check ChexSystems, a reporting agency that records closed accounts, unpaid overdrafts and suspected fraud. Negative records stay for about five years.
You are entitled to one free ChexSystems report every 12 months, online, by mail or by phone (800-428-9623). If something is wrong, dispute it; the agency generally has 30 days to investigate.
Paying off an old overdraft balance at the bank that reported it can help, and you can ask that bank to update the record.
Meanwhile, look for second-chance or Bank On certified accounts. Many do not screen as strictly, and none allow overdraft fees. Wells Fargo Clear Access Banking and Chase Secure Banking are examples.
steps: Request your free ChexSystems report.
Dispute anything inaccurate; pay or settle valid old balances and get it in writing.
Apply for a Bank On certified or second-chance account in the meantime.
entries.next_step: Request your free ChexSystems report and apply for a Bank On certified account while you sort it out.

entries.title: Savings accounts and high-yield savings
entries.summary: Keep emergency money in an insured savings account. Online banks often pay several times what big-bank savings pay.
body: A savings account holds money you are not spending this week, like an emergency fund or money for a goal. It is FDIC or NCUA insured like checking, but it earns interest, shown as APY (annual percentage yield).

Big-bank savings accounts often pay close to nothing. Online banks usually pay much more. For example, Ally Bank listed a 3.10% APY on its online savings account with no minimum and no monthly fee as of October 5, 2026. Rates are variable and change often.

Many savings accounts limit how many withdrawals you can make each month (Ally allows up to 10 per statement cycle), so keep spending money in checking. Many people begin by saving one month of expenses and then building to three to six months.
steps: Open a no-fee, insured savings account; it can be at a different bank from your checking.
Set up an automatic transfer on payday, even a small amount.
Compare APYs once or twice a year; moving savings is free and takes a few days.
entries.next_step: Open a no-fee high-yield savings account and set a small automatic transfer for payday.

entries.title: CDs (certificates of deposit)
entries.summary: Lock money away for a set term, from a few months to five years, at a fixed rate. Taking it out early costs a penalty.
body: A CD is a deposit you agree to leave alone for a fixed term in exchange for a fixed rate. CDs at banks and credit unions (where they may be called share certificates) are insured up to the same $250,000 limit.
Withdrawing before the term ends usually costs an early-withdrawal penalty, often a few months of interest. Read the penalty before you open one.
A common approach is a CD ladder: split the money into several CDs that mature at different times (for example 6, 12 and 18 months) so some of it becomes available regularly.
When a CD matures, many banks automatically renew it for the same term at the current rate unless you act within a short grace period. Put the maturity date on your calendar.
entries.next_step: Only use money you won't need before the term ends; compare the rate and the early-withdrawal penalty at two or three banks.

entries.title: Sudden money: a lottery win, inheritance or settlement
entries.summary: Slow down. Secure the money or ticket, learn your state's privacy rules, assemble a fee-only advisor, CPA and attorney, and make no big promises or purchases for months.
body: Stories of lottery winners who did well have the same early steps: protect the ticket (sign it and store it safely), say nothing publicly, and don't rush to claim.
Some states let winners stay anonymous or claim through a trust; others don't. Check your state's rules before claiming.

Taxes come first: the IRS generally requires 24% federal withholding on large lottery prizes, but the top tax rate is higher, so many winners owe more at tax time. Lump sum versus annuity changes the tax picture; a CPA can model both.

Build a team before deciding anything: a fee-only fiduciary advisor, a CPA and an estate attorney. Put the money somewhere insured and boring while you plan, and wait several months before big gifts, loans or purchases.
steps: Secure the ticket, check or settlement documents, and tell almost no one.
Look up your state's rules on claim deadlines and anonymity.
Hire a fee-only fiduciary, a CPA and an estate attorney.
Park the money in insured accounts and make no big decisions for six months.
entries.next_step: Before claiming anything large, book one meeting with a fee-only fiduciary and a CPA.

entries.title: Helping family financially without losing control
entries.summary: In 2026 you can give $19,000 per person per year with no paperwork and $15 million over a lifetime before tax. Trusts, annuities and 529 plans let gifts help for years.
body: For 2026, each person can give up to $19,000 to any number of people with nothing to file ($38,000 for a married couple giving together). Above that, you file Form 709 and the excess counts against a lifetime exemption of $15 million per person; tax is only owed once that is used up.

To help someone over years without handing over a lump sum: an irrevocable trust with a professional trustee can pay out only income or a set amount; an immediate annuity turns a sum into guaranteed payments; custodial accounts and 529 education plans keep control with a custodian or owner, and 529 withdrawals for non-education costs face tax plus a 10% penalty.
Keep a written record of every gift (date, amount, "this is a gift"), even under the limit, so it isn't later treated as a loan. Explain uneven gifts to family while you can.

Banks report cash deposits over $10,000 automatically; that's routine, not a penalty. Splitting deposits to avoid the report (structuring) is illegal. Gifts keep the giver's cost basis, while inherited assets usually get a step-up to their value at death, which can change taxes a lot.
entries.next_step: Write a one-line record for any gift you've made this year, and talk to an estate attorney before setting up a trust.

entries.title: Moving from trading time to building assets
entries.summary: Higher incomes usually come from leverage: other people's time, systems, communication and capital. Motivational versions of this idea are common; the solid core is simple.
body: A popular teaching (from speakers like Myron Golden) describes levels of value: doing the work yourself, managing people who do it, communicating to many people at once, and creating ideas or systems. Each level multiplies output beyond your own hours.
The solid core: income grows when your effort is multiplied, by a team, by software, by content that keeps working, or by capital invested in things that produce cash.
Wealth comes from assets you own: a business that runs without you, investments, property, a body of work. A high income without assets still stops when you stop.
Be careful with the promises around this idea. "Make your yearly income every month" is a slogan, not a plan. Build one asset at a time, starting with an emergency fund and retirement savings.
entries.next_step: Pick one task you repeat every week and decide whether a person, a system or a template could do it.

entries.title: Depositing a check: when the money is actually yours
entries.summary: By federal rule, the first $275 of most check deposits must be available by the next business day. Weekends do not count.
body: Federal Regulation CC sets the maximum time a bank can hold a deposited check. The dollar amounts were updated on July 1, 2025 and change every five years. Some older pages still show the previous $225 and $5,525 figures.

For most checks, the first $275 must be available no later than the next business day, and the rest usually within two business days. When checks deposited in one day total more than $6,725, the bank may hold the amount over $6,725 for longer, up to about nine business days. New accounts (open less than 30 days) and checks the bank believes may not be paid can also get longer holds.

Business days are Monday through Friday, excluding federal holidays. A check deposited on Saturday night counts as deposited on Monday, so the first $275 usually shows up Tuesday. Your bank's own policy is often faster than the legal maximum; Chase, for example, typically makes deposits made before 11 PM Eastern on a business day available the next business day.
ATM or mobile app? Both usually follow the same schedule. An ATM receipt can show what is available right away, which an app may not. Never deposit the same check both ways.
steps: Sign the back of the check. For mobile deposit, many banks also require a line such as "For mobile deposit only".
Deposit before your bank's daily cutoff on a business day.
Check the ATM receipt or the app's deposit confirmation for the hold schedule.
If money is due before the hold ends, ask the person you owe for a short extension, or call your bank and ask whether it can release part of the hold.
tags: when will my money be available

details.Weekends and holidays: Do not count as business days

entries.next_step: Deposit before your bank's cutoff on a business day and read the hold notice on your receipt.

entries.title: Pending, available and current balance: why the numbers don't match
entries.summary: Your available balance is what you can spend now. Pending charges and held deposits are why it can differ from the balance you expect.
body: Most banking apps show two numbers. The current (or ledger) balance counts everything that has posted. The available balance subtracts pending card charges and deposit holds and adds deposits the bank has already released. The available balance is the one that decides whether a purchase goes through.

A pending transaction is approved but not yet final. Card purchases often post one to three business days later, and some, such as gas, hotels and restaurant tips, can post for a different amount than the pending one.

Overnight processing runs on business days, so weekend transactions often appear all at once on Monday or Tuesday. That is why an account can look fine on Saturday and show an overdraft notice on Monday.

If a transaction seems wrong or you can't figure it out, look at the transaction detail in the app and then call the bank. If the bank doesn't resolve an error, you can file a complaint with the CFPB.

details.Available balance: What you can spend right now
details.Pending: Approved but not final; can change amount

entries.next_step: Turn on low-balance and large-transaction alerts in your bank's app so surprises show up the same day.

entries.title: Overdrafts: how to stop paying for them
entries.summary: Choose an account with no overdraft fees, link a backup savings account, or turn on alerts. Big-bank overdraft fees still run around $34.
body: An overdraft happens when a payment goes through even though your available balance can't cover it. At banks that still charge for it, the fee is often around $34 per item; Bankrate lists Chase's at $34.

Ways to avoid it: use an account with no overdraft fees (any Bank On certified account, Capital One 360, Chase Secure Banking, Wells Fargo Clear Access); link a savings account as automatic backup; use a cushion like Chase's, which charges no fee if you are overdrawn $50 or less; and turn on low-balance alerts.
For everyday debit card and ATM transactions, banks must get your opt-in before charging overdraft fees. If you never opted in, those transactions are simply declined.
entries.next_step: Check whether you opted in to overdraft coverage, and switch it off or move to a no-overdraft account.

entries.title: Sending money: PayPal, Wise and international transfers
entries.summary: Payment apps are fast but final. International transfers come with federal rights: a fee and rate disclosure, a 30-minute cancellation window and 180 days to report errors.
body: Apps like PayPal move money between people quickly, and moving a balance to your bank instantly usually costs a fee that the app shows before you confirm. Standard transfers are slower and often free. Payments to people you don't know are very hard to get back.

For international transfers, services like Wise must show you the fee, the exchange rate and the amount the recipient will get before you pay. You can cancel for a full refund within 30 minutes unless the money has already been picked up or deposited. You also have 180 days to report an error. Complaints can go to the CFPB or your state regulator.

Wise's own payment screen warns that fraudulent transactions may result in the loss of money with no recourse. That is the key point: if someone you have never met in person asks you to receive money and send it on, stop. See the money mule entry.

details.Before paying: Fee, rate and amount received are shown
details.Biggest risk: Sending to strangers is usually final

entries.next_step: Only send to people you know in real life, and read the amount the recipient will get before you confirm.

entries.title: Creator money: income versus ownership
entries.summary: Big creators show the gap between income and wealth: ad and sponsorship income stops when posting stops, while equity in a product or company can grow, but isn't cash in the bank.
body: Most creator income is rented: platform ad revenue, sponsorships and brand deals depend on continuing to post. Reporting on several top creators shows income dropping sharply once they slow down, because nothing underneath runs without them.

Some creators turn attention into ownership: consumer products, food brands, media companies. Reporting on MrBeast's companies describes him as a billionaire on paper while saying in early 2026 that he had little cash, because nearly all of his worth is equity in businesses he keeps reinvesting in.

The reported decision by iShowSpeed to turn down a large guaranteed platform deal is usually explained the same way: keeping control of the audience and the upside rather than trading it for a fixed sum.
The lessons for anyone building an audience: own your customer list, reinvest before you cash out, and remember that equity isn't liquidity. Paper value can't pay rent.

details.Paradox: Rich on paper, short on cash

entries.next_step: Start collecting emails or phone numbers from your audience so you own the relationship, not just the platform followers.

entries.title: The 2008 crisis in plain words (The Big Short)
entries.summary: Risky home loans were bundled into securities, rated as safe, and bet on many times over with derivatives. When borrowers defaulted, losses spread through the whole system.
body: Lenders made many mortgages to borrowers who couldn't afford them, often with low teaser rates that later jumped. Brokers earned commissions on volume, so loan quality fell.

Those loans were pooled into mortgage-backed securities and sliced into layers (tranches), then re-pooled into CDOs. Rating agencies gave much of it top ratings, so investors treated risky debt as safe.

Credit default swaps worked like insurance on that debt. A small group of investors, including Steve Eisman's team, studied the loans themselves, saw rising defaults and bought protection that paid off when the market collapsed. Bets layered on bets meant a dollar of mortgage losses could become many dollars of losses elsewhere.

The lessons for ordinary people: read what you're signing, be wary of loans whose payment can jump, don't assume a rating or a big institution means safety, and remember that real people lose homes, jobs and retirement savings when a bubble breaks.

details.Failure: Ratings treated risky debt as safe
details.Lesson: Read the loan; payments that can jump are a risk

entries.next_step: If you have an adjustable-rate loan, find the date and size of the next possible payment change.

entries.title: Leverage and margin calls: how one trader sank a 233-year-old bank
entries.summary: Borrowed money magnifies losses as well as gains. Barings collapsed in 1995 after one trader hid about £827 million in losses and kept paying margin calls to keep losing bets alive.
body: Leverage means using borrowed money or derivatives to control a bigger position than your cash alone. It magnifies both gains and losses.
A margin call is a demand for more cash when a leveraged position moves against you. Paying it doesn't create profit; it just keeps the losing bet open another day.

Nick Leeson, a trader at Barings Bank in Singapore, hid losses in an error account numbered 88888 and requested more and more cash from London to meet margin calls. By February 1995 the losses were about £827 million, and Britain's oldest merchant bank collapsed. The deeper failure was weak controls: the same person ran trading and checked his own records.
For individuals, the same mechanics apply to margin accounts, options and leveraged crypto products. Never borrow to invest money you can't afford to lose, and never "double down" to win back losses.
entries.next_step: If you trade on margin, find your broker's maintenance requirement and the price at which you'd get a margin call.

entries.title: Soros and reflexivity: why markets overshoot
entries.summary: George Soros argued that market prices don't just reflect reality, they change it. Beliefs and prices feed each other into booms and busts.
body: In The Alchemy of Finance, Soros argues that markets are made of thinking participants whose beliefs affect the very things they're trying to predict. He called this reflexivity.

A rising price can make a company look stronger (easier borrowing, more confidence), which pushes the price higher still, until the gap between belief and reality gets too large and the trend reverses, often sharply.
He also stressed fallibility: every model of the market is incomplete, and a faulty model followed with confidence can be more dangerous than none.
For everyday investors, the practical takeaway is humility: booms feel permanent from the inside, and diversification and position size matter more than certainty.

details.Idea: Beliefs and prices feed each other

entries.next_step: Check whether any single investment is a large share of your savings, and decide your maximum in writing.

entries.title: What legendary traders really teach (it isn't how to get rich fast)
entries.summary: Paul Tudor Jones, David Tepper and Ken Griffin are famous for big wins, but their careers are mostly about controlling risk, buying when others panic, and building systems.
body: Paul Tudor Jones is famous for profiting around the October 1987 crash, when the Dow fell about 22% in a day. He is equally known for emphasizing defense: cutting losing positions and protecting capital first.
David Tepper made his name buying the debt and stock of banks in 2009 that the market believed were finished. It required deep research and a willingness to lose the money if he was wrong.

Ken Griffin built Citadel and Citadel Securities into giants partly by buying distressed portfolios from failing funds, and by market making, which drew public scrutiny during the 2021 GameStop episode.

None of this is a strategy for ordinary savers. Professionals have research teams, risk systems and capital they can afford to lose. The useful lessons are simpler: limit losses, avoid panic selling, and be wary of documentaries that end with a link to a trading app or a book.

details.Tepper lesson: Research, then act when others panic

entries.next_step: If you invest, write down in advance what loss would make you stop and reassess.

entries.title: Jack Ma and the cancelled IPO: when regulators change the rules
entries.summary: In 2020, days after Jack Ma publicly criticized Chinese financial regulators, Ant Group's record IPO was halted. Alibaba later received an 18.2 billion yuan antitrust fine.
body: In late October 2020, Alibaba founder Jack Ma gave a speech in Shanghai criticizing China's financial regulators and comparing banks to pawnshops. Ant Group, his fintech company behind Alipay, was days away from what was expected to be the world's largest IPO.

Regulators summoned Ant's leaders and the listing was suspended in early November 2020. Ma largely disappeared from public view for months. In April 2021, regulators fined Alibaba 18.2 billion yuan (about $2.8 billion) for abusing its market position, and Ant was required to restructure.

Ant's lending model connected huge amounts of consumer and small-business credit to data on hundreds of millions of users, which put it squarely in the path of regulators worried about financial risk and control of data.
The business lessons: regulatory and political risk can outweigh any business model, concentration of power invites scrutiny, and public comments by a founder can move billions.

details.Lesson: Regulatory risk can outweigh the model

entries.next_step: List the rules or regulators your own business depends on, and what you'd do if one changed.

entries.title: AI agents, stablecoins and 'the machine economy'
entries.summary: Big firms and crypto founders are discussing AI agents that pay for data and services by themselves. It's an early idea; treat investment pitches built on it with care.
body: Recent reports from asset managers and crypto research firms describe a future where software agents buy data, computing power and services automatically, often using stablecoins or new payment standards.
Open problems remain: proving a service was actually delivered, handling disputes, fraud, and who is liable when an agent makes a bad purchase.
Videos on the topic are frequently made by founders of companies in that space, who say so in their descriptions. That's fine, but it means they're promoting their own projects.

For most people, the practical point is that money moved by stablecoins or crypto apps generally lacks the protections of an insured bank account, and new technology doesn't change the old rules about speculation.

details.Protection: Usually less than a bank account

entries.next_step: Before using any crypto or stablecoin app, find out whether balances are insured and how disputes are handled.

entries.title: Short on rent or a bill before money clears
entries.summary: What people usually do when a payment is due before a deposit is available, from cheapest to most expensive.
body: This happens to almost everyone: a check arrives on a Saturday, rent is due tonight, and the deposit won't be available until Tuesday. The order below starts with the options that cost nothing.

First, contact whoever you owe. Many landlords and billers will give a few days' grace or waive a late fee if you ask before the deadline and say when the money will arrive. Get any agreement in writing, even a text.

Second, ask your bank. Some banks will release part of a check hold for an established customer, and some offer a small, low-cost advance to existing customers. Third, a short loan from someone you trust, with a clear repayment date, costs nothing but a conversation.

If you need to borrow, a credit union payday alternative loan (PAL) caps the interest at 28% APR, with amounts from $200 up to $2,000 depending on the type. Payday loans and paycheck advance apps with tips and fees usually cost far more. Nonprofit credit counselors can help if this keeps happening.
steps: Message the landlord or biller before the deadline with the amount and the date funds clear.
Call your bank and ask whether it can release part of the hold.
Borrow from someone you trust, with a written repayment date.
If you must borrow formally, ask a credit union about a payday alternative loan.

details.Cheapest: Ask the payee for a short grace period
details.Also free: Ask your bank to release part of a hold

entries.next_step: Message whoever you owe before the deadline and tell them the exact date your money clears.

entries.title: How to find and check out a financial advisor
entries.summary: Know the three main types, look them up on BrokerCheck and IAPD, and ask exactly how they get paid.
body: "Financial advisor" is not a protected title, so anyone can use it. What matters is registration. Brokers are registered with FINRA and sell investments. Registered investment advisers (RIAs) are registered with the SEC or a state, owe you a fiduciary duty and typically charge a fee. A CERTIFIED FINANCIAL PLANNER (CFP) has passed an exam and agreed to CFP Board standards.

Before you meet anyone, look them up. The SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) site and FINRA BrokerCheck show licenses, the firm and any disciplinary history. The SEC warns that unlicensed, unregistered people commit much of the investment fraud in the U.S.
Ask for Form CRS, a short plain-English summary every registered firm must give you that explains services, fees and conflicts of interest.

Ask how they are paid: a flat or hourly fee, a percentage of assets, or commissions on products they sell. Fee-only planners who charge hourly or a flat fee are a common choice for people who want advice without being sold a product.
steps: Find candidates on CFP Board's Let's Make a Plan directory or through referrals.
Look up each person on IAPD (adviserinfo.sec.gov) and BrokerCheck.
Ask for Form CRS and a written list of every fee.
Interview at least two before you sign anything.

details.Ask for: Form CRS and a written fee list

entries.next_step: Look up any advisor's name on IAPD and BrokerCheck before your first meeting.

entries.title: Nonprofit credit counseling for debt
entries.summary: Certified nonprofit counselors help with budgets and debt, and can set up a debt management plan with lower interest.
body: If debt is piling up, a nonprofit credit counselor is usually the first call. The National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC) connects you with certified counselors by phone, video or online.

A counselor reviews your income, bills and debts and builds a plan. If it makes sense, they can set up a debt management plan (DMP): one monthly payment to the agency, which pays your creditors, often at reduced interest rates and with collection calls stopped.
Be careful with for-profit "debt settlement" companies that tell you to stop paying your bills and charge large fees. A nonprofit counselor will explain the trade-offs.
entries.next_step: Call the NFCC at 877-360-6322 or request a counselor on nfcc.org.

entries.title: HUD-approved housing counselors (renting, buying, foreclosure)
entries.summary: Free or low-cost, independent help with renting, buying a first home, falling behind on a mortgage or avoiding foreclosure.
body: HUD approves nonprofit housing counseling agencies across the country. Their counselors give independent advice, often at little or no cost, on renting, buying a home, loan defaults, forbearance, foreclosure and credit problems.
Search by ZIP code on the CFPB's housing counselor finder, or call the CFPB at 855-411-2372.
If you are behind on a mortgage, call a counselor before you sign anything with a company that charges upfront fees to "save" your home.
entries.next_step: Enter your ZIP on the CFPB housing counselor finder.

entries.title: Free tax preparation (VITA and TCE)
entries.summary: IRS-certified volunteers prepare returns for free if you earn about $70,244 or less, or are 60 or older.
body: VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) prepares basic tax returns for free for people who generally earn $70,244 or less, people with disabilities and people with limited English. Individual sites may set their own limits.
TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) focuses on people 60 and older, with expertise in pensions and retirement questions. Many TCE sites are run by AARP Foundation Tax-Aide.
Volunteers must pass IRS tax-law training, and every return gets a quality review before it is filed. Find a site with the IRS VITA locator or call 800-906-9887.
entries.next_step: Use the IRS VITA locator to find a free site near you before tax season fills up.

entries.title: When a bank won't fix it: file a CFPB complaint
entries.summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sends your complaint to the company, which usually responds within 15 days.
body: Start with the company: call, then send a written message that lays out the problem, the dates and the amounts. If that doesn't work, the CFPB takes complaints about bank accounts, money transfers, credit cards, credit reports, debt collection, mortgages and more.

Filing online takes about 10 minutes, and you can attach up to 50 pages of documents. The CFPB forwards the complaint to the company, most companies respond within 15 days, and a version without personal details goes into a public database.
You can also call 855-411-2372, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern. For credit report errors, dispute directly with the credit bureau first.
entries.next_step: Write down dates and amounts, contact the company once more in writing, then file at consumerfinance.gov/complaint.

entries.title: Free help for small businesses: SCORE, SBDCs and more
entries.summary: Free mentoring from SCORE volunteers, low-cost advising at Small Business Development Centers, and SBA resources cover most early questions.
body: SCORE is a nonprofit network of volunteer business mentors, supported by the SBA, offering free one-on-one mentoring and workshops in person and online.

Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), often hosted by universities and colleges, give free or low-cost advising on business plans, financing, marketing and more. Women's Business Centers and Veterans Business Outreach Centers serve specific groups.
Your local library often has free business databases, and many cities have small-business offices with grants, permits help and events.
Paid coaching and courses can be useful later. Start with the free options and bring specific questions.
entries.next_step: Request a free SCORE mentor or book an SBDC appointment with one specific question.

entries.title: Is my money insured? FDIC and NCUA basics
entries.summary: Bank and credit union deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category. Investments and crypto are not.
body: The FDIC insures deposits at member banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category (single, joint, retirement and so on). The NCUA does the same for federally insured credit unions. Since 1933, no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds.

Covered: checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, CDs and cashier's checks. Not covered: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, crypto, annuities, life insurance, safe deposit box contents and Treasury securities.

Many apps are fintechs, not banks. Their deposits are insured only through a partner bank and only once the money is actually held there. Novo, for example, says plainly that it is a fintech and its banking services are provided by Middlesex Federal Savings, F.A., Member FDIC. Payment-app balances (such as a PayPal or Wise balance) work differently from a bank account, so read each app's terms.

details.Limit: $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category
details.Not covered: Stocks, crypto, annuities, safe deposit boxes

entries.next_step: Look up your bank, or an app's partner bank, on FDIC BankFind.

entries.title: Money mule scams: never pass money along for someone
entries.summary: If someone sends you money and asks you to forward it, convert it or send it overseas, you may be moving stolen funds, and you can be held responsible.
body: A money mule is anyone who receives and moves money at someone else's direction, whether or not they know it came from a crime. Scammers recruit through online relationships, job posts for "payment processing" or "financial assistant" roles, and friendly strangers who need a favor.

Warning signs: a deposit from someone you have never met in person; a request to forward most of it by wire, Wise, gift cards or crypto and keep a small cut; pressure to move fast; or money arriving from several unrelated people.
The consequences fall on the middleman: frozen bank and app accounts, being ordered to repay victims, damaged banking history and possible criminal charges.

If you think it has happened to you: stop moving money, do not send anything back to the person, contact your bank and the payment apps involved, and report it to the FBI at IC3.gov and the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
steps: Stop: do not send, forward or return any money.
Call your bank and each app involved (PayPal, Wise and so on).
Report at IC3.gov and ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Save every message, receipt and screenshot.

details.Red flag: Receive money, keep a cut, send the rest on
details.Who pays: The middleman can lose accounts and face charges

entries.next_step: If this sounds familiar, stop all transfers and call your bank today.

entries.title: "Turn your 401(k) into gold": what to check first
entries.summary: Gold IRA ads are sales funnels. The CFTC warns of spreads over 300%, heavy fees and unregistered salespeople.
body: Ads that promise to "protect your retirement" by moving a 401(k) into physical gold usually lead to a free guide in exchange for your name, email and phone number, and then a sales call. Star ratings and testimonials on the page are marketing, not independent checks.

The CFTC's checklist explains what to look for. The spread is the gap between what a dealer sells metal for and what it will buy it back for; some fraudulent dealers have charged spreads above 300%. Ask for every fee in writing and compare the price to metal weight × the spot price. Gold IRAs are self-directed IRAs, so storage, custodian and insurance fees add up, and custodians do not check whether an investment is good.

Be wary of "semi-numismatic" or collectible coins pushed as investments. The term has no special meaning, and the markups are high. Regulated exchange-traded products are another way people get gold exposure, often at lower cost.
Before moving any retirement money, talk to a fee-only fiduciary who sells no metals, and check the salesperson's registration.

details.Ask for: All fees in writing; price vs. spot
details.Second opinion: Fee-only fiduciary who sells no metals

entries.next_step: Before moving retirement money, get a second opinion from a fee-only fiduciary and read the CFTC's 10 questions.

SEC Investor Alert — Self-directed IRAs and the risk of fraud

entries.title: AI trading software and "proven accuracy" claims
entries.summary: A high accuracy number is not a win rate. Read who paid for the study and what the fine print says about hypothetical results.
body: Trading-software sites often lead with one big number, such as "77% accurate" or "87.6% on some stocks." Look at what is being predicted. One popular product measures whether a three-day moving average will be higher or lower two days later, which is a much easier target than predicting a profitable trade.

That product's own disclaimer says an 80% accuracy figure does not mean 8 out of 10 trades will win. It also says hypothetical results are prepared with hindsight, involve no real financial risk, and that the company has had little or no experience trading actual accounts.
Check who paid for any "independent" study. The accuracy analysis in this folder is labeled a third-party study, but its copyright belongs to the software company.
Before paying for any trading tool, read the full disclaimer, ask for audited real-money results, and remember that most people are better served by a fee-only planner than by signals.

details.Fine print: Hypothetical results are made with hindsight

entries.next_step: Read the full disclaimer page and ask for audited real-account results before paying for any trading software.

sources.label: Investor.gov — Check out your investment professional

entries.title: Trading newsletters that promise to beat the market
entries.summary: "Multiple times the S&P's return, year after year" is a sales claim. Check registration and look for guarantees, urgency and upsells.
body: Options and trading newsletters often follow the same script: a founder story ("I didn't have the traditional Wall Street path"), a put-down of index funds ("barely enough to keep up"), and a promise that you can earn several times the market's return every year.
Sustained returns several times the market's, year after year, are extraordinarily rare. Claims of guaranteed or risk-free profits are, in the SEC's words, hallmarks of fraud.

Before you pay: search the person and firm on BrokerCheck and IAPD (many newsletter writers are not registered and are not allowed to give personalized advice), read the refund and auto-renewal terms, and watch for a free tier that exists to sell a higher-priced "inner circle".
If you want to learn to invest, free education from Investor.gov and FINRA covers the same basics without a sales funnel.

details.Red flag: Returns several times the market, every year

entries.next_step: Look up the writer and firm on BrokerCheck before subscribing.

entries.title: Buyer's remorse: your options after a purchase you regret
entries.summary: Start with the store's return policy. Sales made at your home can often be cancelled within three business days, and card purchases can be disputed in some cases.
body: Buyer's remorse usually hits after a big purchase made fast. Your options depend on where and how you bought.

Store and online purchases: there is no general federal right to return them, so the seller's return policy decides. Read it, act within its window and keep the item in like-new condition with packaging and receipt.

Sales at your home, workplace or a temporary location (a hotel, fair or convention): the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule usually gives you until midnight of the third business day to cancel. It covers sales of $25 or more at home and $130 or more at temporary locations, but not online, mail or phone orders, real estate, insurance, securities or cars. Send the cancellation form by certified mail; the seller must refund you within 10 days.

Paid by credit card and the item wasn't delivered as promised? You can dispute the charge with your card issuer. To prevent remorse next time: sleep on any big purchase overnight, read the return policy before paying, and compare at least one alternative.
steps: Find the receipt and the return policy; note the deadline.
Contact the seller in writing and ask for a return or refund.
If it was a door-to-door or event sale, use the Cooling-Off Rule within three business days.
If the seller won't help and you paid by card, ask your card issuer about a dispute.
entries.next_step: Read the return policy today and contact the seller in writing before the window closes.

entries.title: How a subscription supplement funnel works (and where the risk sits)
entries.summary: A hook video, a 'free plus shipping' trial, a near-zero checkout, then four upsells and a recurring plan. Learn to spot the 15 patterns, and the billing and claims rules behind them.
body: The route usually runs: a dark page with one video and one promise, a free trial for the price of shipping, a three-step checkout with a near-zero total, an onboarding page that doubles as an upsell, a smaller offer for anyone who said no, then upgrades, a daily add-on, a topical product and a big-ticket item with a payment-plan fallback.
The main video often follows nine beats: pattern break, authority, a common enemy, an origin story, a mechanism, proof, the offer, risk reversal and a call to action.

Patterns worth recognizing: open loops, single focus, borrowed authority, named comments, free plus shipping, three packages with struck-through prices, "free" bonus units, installment downsells, interruption framing ("wait, your order isn't complete"), deadline wording and quiet declines (a tiny "no thanks" link beside a big "yes" button).

Where the legal risk sits: a free trial that turns into a monthly plan is a negative option. Under the federal ROSCA law, sellers must clearly disclose the terms before taking billing details, get express consent and provide a simple way to stop charges. Supplement claims about body structure or function need substantiation and the FDA disclaimer, and may not claim to treat or cure disease. Fake or unrepresentative testimonials are prohibited.
As a buyer: read the order summary, look for the recurring charge and how to cancel before entering a card, and use a card you can dispute.

details.Buyer tip: Find the recurring charge before paying

entries.next_step: Before entering a card on any trial offer, find the recurring price and the cancel instructions in writing.

sources.label: FTC — Negative option rule and ROSCA

entries.title: "Cash from your home, no monthly payments": home equity agreement ads
entries.summary: These ads promote home equity contracts: cash now, one large repayment later tied to your home's value. 'No monthly payments' describes when you pay, not how much.
body: A common funnel runs from a story-style email to an article-looking page, an amount picker and a hand-off to a provider. The product is often a home equity agreement (regulators also call it a home equity contract or investment).

You receive cash now. Later, at the end of a term that can run 10 to 30 years or when you sell, you repay one lump sum based partly on your home's value. California's regulator has warned the provider's share can be as high as 70% of the home's value or its increase.

Watch for the marketing patterns: advertising dressed as news without a clear "advertisement" label, testimonials showing best-case payouts, paid relationships disclosed only in the footer, and a headline maximum amount that few people get.

Before signing anything secured by your home, ask for the repayment formula with an example, all fees, and what happens if you can't repay, and talk to a HUD-approved housing counselor for an independent opinion.

details.Repay: Lump sum later, tied to home value

entries.next_step: Ask the provider for a written repayment example at your home's value, then review it with a housing counselor.

entries.title: Meme coins and viral trading stories
entries.summary: Stories of students turning a few hundred dollars into millions spread fast, but often can't be verified, and every big winner in a hype coin is paid by later buyers who lose.
body: One widely shared story claimed a college student made about $40 million trading a celebrity meme coin in a weekend. A documentary on it notes no public wallet ever confirmed the trade; the legend outran the evidence.

The same documentary reports that the coin lost about three quarters of its value within weeks and more than 90% within about a year and a half. The money winners made came from people who bought near the top.
Meme coins have no cash flow or underlying business; the price depends only on attention. Insiders and early wallets often hold large shares and can sell into the hype.

Crypto held on exchanges isn't FDIC insured. If you speculate at all, use only money you can afford to lose completely, and be very skeptical of anyone selling "1000× multiplier" trading apps in a video's description.
entries.next_step: Before buying any token, find out who holds the largest wallets and how much they could sell.

entries.title: The 'client' who pays from someone else's account
entries.summary: A new client you only know online pays you from a stranger's account, then asks you to send money on to relatives. You may be moving stolen funds, and the losses can land on you.
body: A pattern that catches freelancers and small businesses: a client met through a messaging app hires you for real-looking work, such as website maintenance, but payments arrive from different people or organizations than the client.

Then come requests: "I overpaid, please send the difference back," or "please forward part of this to my family overseas." Later, the real account holder disputes the payment, the money is pulled back, and whatever you forwarded is gone.

Red flags: payers who don't match the client's name, a foreign phone number and no video calls, urgency, requests to use Wise, gift cards or crypto, and an email from an organization saying it never hired you.

If this sounds familiar: stop all work and transfers, return any disputed payment only through the payment app's refund button on the original transaction, contact the platforms and your bank, report it at IC3.gov and ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and keep every message. A lawyer can advise you on your own exposure.
steps: Stop sending money and pause the work.
Refund disputed payments only to the original payer, through the platform.
Call PayPal, Wise or your bank, and report at IC3.gov and ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Save every message and invoice; consider a lawyer.

details.The ask: Send money back or on to others

entries.title: Using someone else's credit for a loan (straw borrowers)
entries.summary: Having a relative or friend 'be the front face' on a loan that's really for you can be loan fraud for both of you, even if everyone agrees and the payments get made.
body: Some wealth-building talks describe getting a loan approved by having someone with better credit sign as the borrower while the money really goes to someone else, sometimes with a cash payment for their help.

Lenders call this a straw borrower or straw buyer. Misrepresenting who the real borrower is, or who will live in a property, on a loan application can be mortgage or bank fraud, and the person who signed owes the debt in full.
Legitimate alternatives exist: a co-signer or co-borrower who is honestly disclosed and understands they're fully responsible, a smaller loan, rebuilding your own credit, or seller financing.
If someone offers to "rent" you their credit, or asks to borrow yours, say no and talk to a HUD-approved housing counselor or nonprofit credit counselor instead.

details.Risk: Fraud; the signer owes it all

entries.next_step: If you need a co-signer, have the lender explain in writing exactly what that person is responsible for.

entries.title: Judging 'make money online' income claims
entries.summary: Screenshots of dashboards, luxury rentals and 'I made $X in 90 days' titles are marketing. Ask what's being sold, who profits, and what typical results look like.
body: Many money-making videos follow a script: a big number in the title, a dashboard screenshot, a lifestyle moment, then links to the presenter's paid prompts, course, coaching or software, often with commission disclosures in the description.

Questions to ask: What is actually being sold? Does the presenter profit if I buy the tools they recommend? Are typical results shown, or only the best case? Is the income from the method itself, or from selling the method?
The FTC treats unsubstantiated earnings claims in business opportunity marketing seriously and has warned consumers about programs promising easy income.
Plenty of these videos contain useful tactics. Take the tactics, ignore the income promises, and never pay for "done-for-you" income systems you can't verify.

details.Ask: What's being sold, and who profits?

entries.next_step: Before buying a course, search its name with the words "refund" and "complaint" and read the full refund policy.

entries.title: Fake 'official' notices aimed at new businesses
entries.summary: New LLC owners often get letters that look official, demanding fees for annual reports, certificates, labor-law posters or ownership filings. Check the real agency first.
body: Business filings are public, so new owners quickly receive mail and email that imitates government notices: "annual report due", "certificate of good standing", "required labor law posters" or "BOI filing" with large fees and urgent deadlines.
Some are outright scams; others are legal but misleading offers from private companies charging far more than the state does.

Check the sender against your state's official website, look up the real fee, and file directly with the agency. Arizona, for example, doesn't require LLC annual reports at all, and U.S. companies no longer file BOI reports.
An EIN is always free from the IRS. Report imposter notices to your state's attorney general and the FTC.

details.Check: The real agency's website and fee

entries.next_step: When an official-looking notice arrives, look up the agency yourself instead of using the letter's link or phone number.

entries.title: Where the dollar stands today: the live tracker
entries.summary: One page that pulls today's gold price, inflation, interest rates, the national debt, interest costs, the dollar index and GDP straight from official sources, each with its date and a link to check it.
body: There is no single number that tells you what a dollar is "really" worth. The tracker shows several yardsticks side by side so you can judge for yourself: what the dollar buys in gold, what it buys in everyday prices (the CPI), what savers earn after inflation, what the government owes and pays in interest, and how the dollar trades against other currencies.

The headline is the dollar measured in gold, because gold has no interest rate, no central bank and no budget deficit. That makes it a blunt but useful ruler. It is also volatile: gold fell roughly 45% from 2011 to 2015, so the tracker always shows gold next to the CPI rather than on its own.

Every figure comes from a public source: the U.S. Treasury's Fiscal Data site (debt to the penny and the average interest rate on the debt), FRED from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (yields, inflation, the dollar index, GDP, interest payments, money supply) and a spot gold price feed. The page refreshes the numbers every 15 minutes at most. Monthly and quarterly numbers only change when the agency publishes a new release.
steps: Open the Dollar tracker page and start with the gold card and the CPI card side by side.
Check the real return card: if it is negative, safe short-term savings are losing to inflation right now.
Look at the debt and interest cards together. The interest bill matters more than the headline debt.
Click any source link to see the official series and its full history.

details.Sources: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, FRED (St. Louis Fed), spot gold feed

entries.next_step: Open the Dollar tracker and compare the gold card with the CPI card before deciding what the dollar's "real" value means to you.

entries.title: The dollar as the world's reserve currency
entries.summary: Central banks hold dollars and Treasuries as savings, which lets the U.S. borrow cheaply. That demand is slowly shifting toward gold, and some U.S. leaders now question whether the role is worth it.
body: Since the 1944 Bretton Woods agreement, the dollar has been the money the world saves in and trades with. Foreign central banks hold dollar assets, mostly U.S. Treasury bonds, as their reserves. That steady demand keeps U.S. borrowing costs lower than they would otherwise be. It has been called America's "exorbitant privilege."

The trade-off is a strong dollar, which makes U.S.-made goods expensive abroad. In 2023, then-Senator JD Vance called reserve status "a resource curse," comparing it to coal in Appalachia, where the wealth left and the region was left poorer.

The mix is changing. A European Central Bank report covered by the Financial Times found that gold made up about 27% of central bank reserves at the end of 2025, ahead of U.S. Treasuries at about 22%. Dollar assets as a whole were still the largest share at about 42%. Central banks bought more than 1,000 tons of gold a year from 2022 to 2024 after Russia's dollar reserves were frozen, then about 850 tons in 2025.

"De-dollarization" is slow. The dollar is still used in most foreign-exchange trades and much of global trade. The question is not whether it disappears tomorrow, but whether demand for U.S. debt keeps weakening while the U.S. needs to borrow more.
steps: Watch the dollar index card on the tracker: up means a stronger dollar against trading partners.
Watch the 30-year yield: when foreign demand weakens, long-term rates tend to rise.
Read the World Gold Council's central bank data for the latest gold buying.
entries.next_step: Compare the dollar index and the 30-year yield on the Dollar tracker to see whether the dollar is strengthening or borrowing costs are climbing.

World Gold Council — central bank statistics

entries.title: Nominal vs. real: why a bigger balance can buy less
entries.summary: Nominal is the dollar number on your screen. Real is what it buys after inflation. If your money grows slower than prices, you are getting poorer even as the balance rises.
body: If your savings earn 3% and prices rise 4%, your balance goes up but your buying power falls about 1% a year. Economists call that a negative real return.

The same idea applies to investments. A stock index can be up strongly in dollars and flat or down when measured against gold or adjusted for inflation. Andrei Jikh's August 2026 video gave examples: by his figures, the Nasdaq-100 was up about 95% over five years in dollars but down about 23% priced in gold. Those are his numbers and they depend heavily on the dates chosen, but the idea is sound: always ask "up compared with what?"

For everyday life, the CPI is the most common yardstick. The Bureau of Labor Statistics also publishes the "purchasing power of the consumer dollar," which shows what a 1982–84 dollar is worth today in cents.
steps: Find the interest rate on your savings, CD or bond.
Subtract the latest 12-month CPI from the tracker.
If the result is negative, your money is losing buying power. Ask a fiduciary about options.
entries.next_step: Write down what your savings earn and compare it with the CPI card on the Dollar tracker.

sources.label: FRED — Purchasing power of the consumer dollar

entries.title: Gold as a yardstick for the dollar
entries.summary: Pricing things in gold shows how much the dollar has lost against a money no government can print. It is useful, but gold swings hard, so it should be one ruler among several.
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been quoted as saying gold cannot run a budget deficit or fight a war. That is why some people treat gold as a neutral yardstick: if the dollar price of gold triples, the dollar bought a third as much gold.

Gold set a record above $5,500 an ounce in January 2026, as reported by MiningMX, and has since come down. On the tracker, the dollar-in-gold card compares today's spot price with approximate annual average prices for 2000, 2014 and 2020.

Limits: gold pays no interest, has storage and dealer costs, and has had long losing stretches. It fell roughly 45% from 2011 to 2015, and it lost value in real terms for most of the 1980s and 1990s. A gold-priced chart flatters gold during gold booms.
Buying gold is an investment decision. This guide does not recommend it. If you are pitched gold coins or a gold IRA, read the "Turn your 401(k) into gold" warning first.
steps: Check the gold card and the dollar-in-gold card on the tracker.
Compare with the CPI card: if the two disagree, ask why.
Before buying any gold product, compare the dealer's markup with the spot price.
entries.next_step: Open the Dollar tracker's gold cards, then read the gold IRA warning before talking to any dealer.

entries.title: The bond market and why yields matter to you
entries.summary: The Fed steers short-term rates. The market sets long-term ones. When investors demand more to lend for 10 or 30 years, mortgages, car loans and the government's interest bill all get pricier.
body: Treasury bills mature in a year or less, notes in 2 to 10 years and bonds in 20 to 30 years. The yield is the return an investor earns at today's price. When yields rise, existing bond prices fall.

The Federal Reserve sets the overnight fed funds rate, which pulls short-term bill yields along with it. Long-term yields are set at Treasury auctions by pension funds, insurers, banks, hedge funds and foreign buyers.

On August 17, 2026, the 30-year Treasury yield reached about 5.31%, its highest since 2007. Treasury then announced it would at least double its buybacks of long-term bonds, from up to $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation, and said its roughly $950 billion cash account could help fund them. Long-term yields dipped briefly, then rose again.

Treasury has also leaned more on short-term bills, about 22% of marketable debt in late July 2026, which is above the 15–20% range its advisory committee recommends. Bills can be refinanced at lower rates if the Fed cuts, but they also have to be rolled over constantly.

Compare the 3-month bill with the CPI to see the real return on safe savings.

entries.title: The national debt and the interest bill
entries.summary: The debt passed $40 trillion in August 2026, and interest now costs over $1 trillion a year, more than Medicare. You can check the exact number yourself every business day.
body: The Treasury publishes the total public debt every business day ("Debt to the Penny"). It passed $40 trillion on August 18, 2026, at $40.047 trillion, and stood near $40.33 trillion in mid-October. Anyone can download the full history, so claims that the debt did or didn't rise can be checked directly.

There are two parts. Debt held by the public, about $32.5 trillion, is owed to investors, banks, foreign governments and the Federal Reserve. Intragovernmental debt, about $7.8 trillion, is owed to federal trust funds such as Social Security.

The interest bill matters more than the headline number. It is about $1.1 trillion a year, and in fiscal 2026 it passed Medicare to become the second-largest line in the budget after Social Security. In the first 11 months of fiscal 2026, interest costs grew about 12% while tax receipts grew about 3%, according to CBO.

The average interest rate on all marketable Treasury debt was about 3.5% in September 2026. As older, cheaper debt matures and is refinanced at today's higher rates, that average and the interest bill tend to rise.
steps: Open the debt card on the tracker for today's figure and the change over 12 months.
Look at the interest card and the average rate card together.
To check any claim yourself, download Debt to the Penny from fiscaldata.treasury.gov.

entries.title: Inflation and the CPI: what the number does and doesn't show
entries.summary: The CPI tracks the price of a basket of goods and services. It's the official inflation rate, but your own costs, like rent, insurance and groceries, can run hotter or cooler.
body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics prices tens of thousands of items each month across the country. The headline CPI covers everything. "Core" CPI leaves out food and energy because they swing the most.

Common criticisms: the basket adjusts for quality improvements and for people switching to cheaper goods, which some say understates the inflation people feel. Housing is measured partly through estimated rents. BLS publishes its methods and alternative measures, and other indexes, such as the Fed's preferred PCE index, often run a little lower.
If your own costs rise faster than the CPI, the official number won't match your experience. Track your top five monthly costs year over year to see your personal inflation rate.
steps: Read the CPI and core CPI cards on the tracker.
List your five biggest monthly costs and compare them with a year ago.
Use the BLS CPI inflation calculator to see what an old price equals today.
entries.next_step: Compare the tracker's CPI with your own five biggest costs, then try the BLS inflation calculator.

entries.title: Is GDP real? How it's measured and revised
entries.summary: GDP is estimated, then revised several times as better data arrives. The government also measures the same economy from the income side (GDI). Comparing the two is one of the best ways to sanity-check growth.
body: The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes GDP each quarter: an advance estimate about a month after the quarter ends, two more estimates after that, and then annual and multi-year revisions. Early numbers can move a lot.

"Real" GDP removes inflation. Nominal GDP can rise just because prices rose. When people say GDP is "fake," they often mean that a big share of growth comes from government spending, finance or rising asset prices rather than things people can touch. That is a debate about what kind of growth it is. The measurement methods themselves are published.

GDP adds up spending, while GDI adds up incomes. In theory they match. When GDI is much weaker than GDP, economists treat the growth number with more caution. The tracker shows both for the latest quarter.
Other checks on the real economy include jobs and wages, industrial production, electricity use and freight volumes.
steps: Compare the GDP and GDI figures on the tracker's GDP card.
Check whether the latest figure is an advance or a revised estimate at bea.gov.
Look at one physical measure, such as electricity or industrial production, as a cross-check.
entries.next_step: Open the GDP card on the Dollar tracker and compare it with GDI before trusting any single growth headline.

entries.title: Electricity as a gauge of real output
entries.summary: Electricity use is a rough measure of how much physical work an economy does. U.S. generation was roughly flat from about 2007 to 2023, while China's grew to more than twice the U.S. total.
body: Factories, data centers, mines and transit all run on power, so electricity is one way to look past dollar figures. It is a blunt tool: efficiency gains, such as LED lighting, mean you can do more with the same power.

According to Ember's Global Electricity Review 2025, U.S. demand was largely flat for most of the 2010s, then rose 3% in 2024. China's electricity demand in 2024 was about 10,066 TWh, more than twice U.S. generation of roughly 4,300 TWh. The U.S. is now growing again as data centers and manufacturing add load.
The tracker shows the latest annual U.S. generation from the Energy Information Administration when the site owner connects a free EIA key.

entries.title: Stablecoins and the GENIUS Act
entries.summary: Dollar stablecoins are crypto tokens meant to stay worth $1. The GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, requires them to be backed by safe assets such as short-term Treasury bills, which makes stablecoin issuers big buyers of U.S. debt.
body: A payment stablecoin is a digital token that can be redeemed for one dollar. Under the GENIUS Act, issuers must hold reserves such as cash, insured bank deposits, Treasury bills maturing in 93 days or less, short repurchase agreements backed by bills, and government money market funds.

That means every new stablecoin dollar adds demand for short-term U.S. debt. People in countries with failing currencies often want dollars for safety and may hold them without earning interest. Critics argue this gives Washington a large, steady buyer for its bills. Supporters say it extends the dollar's reach and protects consumers with clear rules.
A stablecoin is not a bank deposit and is not FDIC-insured. Read who the issuer is, where reserves are held and how redemption works before holding one.
steps: Check whether a stablecoin's issuer is licensed and publishes regular reserve reports.
Remember that it is not FDIC-insured, so keep emergency money in an insured account.
Watch for rulemaking from Treasury and the bank regulators as the law takes effect.

entries.title: How America shrank its World War II debt: financial repression
entries.summary: After 1945, the U.S. held interest rates below inflation for years. Debt shrank relative to the economy, partly paid for by bondholders whose savings lost buying power.
body: After World War II, U.S. debt was about as large relative to the economy as it is today. Within about a decade it had been roughly cut in half, without being paid off.

Economists Carmen Reinhart and M. Belen Sbrancia call the method "financial repression." Rates were capped (the Fed held Treasury yields down until the 1951 Treasury–Fed Accord), banks and pensions held large amounts of government bonds, and inflation ran above the interest those bonds paid. For the U.S. and U.K., they estimate negative real rates cut debt by 3–4% of GDP a year.
Strong postwar growth did a lot of the work too. Today's economy grows more slowly, and more of the debt is held by foreigners who can sell, so the same playbook would work differently.

Some commentators, including Andrei Jikh in his August 2026 video, argue that a modern version is underway: more short-term borrowing, new captive buyers through stablecoins, and inflation above interest rates. That is an interpretation, not an announced policy. The tracker's real-yield cards show whether real rates are actually negative.
steps: Check the tracker's real return and 10-year real yield cards.
If real rates turn negative and stay there, ask a fiduciary how that affects your savings.

details.Debt reduction: 3–4% of GDP a year (US and UK)

entries.title: Savings built to keep up with inflation: I Bonds and TIPS
entries.summary: The Treasury sells two kinds of savings tied to inflation. I Bonds and TIPS both adjust for the CPI. Learn how they work before deciding whether either fits you.
body: I Bonds are savings bonds whose rate combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate reset every six months. They are bought at TreasuryDirect.gov, generally up to $10,000 a year per person electronically. You can't cash them in for the first 12 months, and cashing in before five years costs the last three months of interest.

TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) are marketable bonds whose principal rises with the CPI. They can be bought at auction through TreasuryDirect or through a brokerage, and their price moves day to day like other bonds. The 10-year TIPS yield on the tracker is the market's "real" interest rate.
Both are tied to the CPI, not to gold or your personal costs. This is information, not a recommendation. A fee-only fiduciary can tell you whether either fits your goals and taxes.
steps: Read the current I Bond rate on TreasuryDirect.gov.
Compare it with high-yield savings and CD rates at insured banks.
Ask a fiduciary or a free VITA tax volunteer about the tax side before buying.

details.I Bond lockup: 12 months; 3 months' interest lost before 5 years

entries.title: Put options "to protect against the dollar": know the risk first
entries.summary: A put option is a contract that rises in value if something falls. It expires, and most of the time you can lose the whole amount you paid. Learn how options work before risking any money.
body: A put gives you the right to sell something at a set price by a set date. If the price falls far enough before expiration, the put gains value. If it doesn't, the put can expire worthless and you lose the whole premium. Timing has to be right, not just direction.

Brokerages must approve you for options trading and give you the official "Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options" booklet. Selling options, rather than buying them, can lose far more than you put in.

Social media often pitches small starting amounts, such as $5 or $500, as a low-risk way in. The amount doesn't change the odds. A small loss is still a total loss of that money. This guide doesn't recommend any trade or amount.
Free education: Investor.gov (SEC) and FINRA explain options with examples. A fee-only fiduciary can tell you whether options make sense for you at all.
steps: Read the options basics from FINRA and Investor.gov before opening any options account.
Practice with a paper-trading account, which uses no real money, if your broker offers one.
Only consider money you can lose completely, and talk to a fiduciary first.

details.Selling options: Can lose more than you put in

entries.title: "The dollar is collapsing" sales pitches
entries.summary: Fear of the dollar's decline is used to sell gold coins, gold IRAs, crypto schemes, newsletters and courses. A real problem doesn't make the product a good deal.
body: The dollar's problems are real enough to talk about, which makes them good marketing. Warning signs: a countdown or deadline, "the banks will freeze your money," a single product presented as the only safe option, coins sold far above the spot gold price, or pressure to move retirement money today.

Many finance videos are sponsored or carry affiliate links, and many end with a paid membership pitch. That doesn't make the content wrong, but it is a reason to check the numbers yourself, which the Dollar tracker helps you do.
The CFTC and FTC warn about precious-metals and investment schemes. If you've already paid, contact your bank or card issuer right away, and report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
steps: Check the live numbers on the Dollar tracker instead of trusting a pitch's numbers.
Compare any gold product's price with the spot price, and ask for all fees in writing.
Never move retirement money on a phone call. Talk to your plan provider and a fiduciary first.
